articles.title: WATCH: Hegseth calls for ‘Peace Through Strength’ in the Pacific
articles.summary: Hegseth’s message to ASEAN: train together, plan together, and stay strong enough to keep conflict at bay.

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 1:23pm

MANILA, Philippines — US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is pushing for stronger defense cooperation between the United States and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), including closer maritime coordination and joint military training.

In his remarks at the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus), Hegseth said the administration of US President Donald Trump envisions a more stable, secure and prosperous Pacific built on strong, self-reliant nations capable of defending their sovereignty.
He described Washington’s approach as “strong, quiet, and clear,” saying the US aims to deter coercion and aggression while avoiding unnecessary escalation.
Hegseth added that the United States would defend its interests as well as those of its allies and partners.
“These are not symbolic things. They are concrete demonstrations of what serious partners do,” Hegseth said.
“Serious partners train together, learn together, plan together, and build the confidence and competence necessary to prevent conflict,” he added.

articles.title: SC orders Senate, House to comment on impeachment voting threshold petition
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has directed the Senate impeachment court and the House of Representatives to comment on a petition filed by Senators Robin Padilla and Bong Go seeking to declare null the ruling on…

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 1:15pm

The Supreme Court has directed the Senate impeachment court and the House of Representatives to comment on a petition filed by Senators Robin Padilla and Bong Go seeking to declare null the ruling on the voting threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte’s conviction.

In a resolution dated October 14, the High Court required the Senate impeachment court---represented by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and court presiding officer Francis Escudero---and the House---represented by Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III and lead prosecutor Rep. Gerville Luistro---to comment on the petition within a non-extendible period of five days.
GMA News Online has reached out to the offices of the respondents and will update this story once they respond.

In a petition for certiorari and prohibition filed earlier this month, Padilla, Go, and the Partido Demokratiko Pilipino-Lakas ng Bayan (PDP-Laban) asked the SC to issue a status quo ante order or a temporary restraining order directing the Impeachment court and the House of Representatives to refrain from excluding any senator from the count of “all members of the Senate” under the Constitution.
The impeachment court earlier voted to base the “two-thirds of votes” on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."
Under the 1987 Constitution, no person shall be convicted in an impeachment trial without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate.

In early September, the impeachment court invited retired Supreme Court Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban, Reynato Puno, and Hilario Davide Jr. and Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna as amici curiae or friends of the court.
Panganiban, Puno, and Davide said that the voting threshold should be based on the number of senator-judges who actively participated in the impeachment trial.

However, Azcuna, one of the framers of the 1987 Constitution, offered a different view that the two-thirds concurrence requirement should relate to the entire membership of the Senate; hence, a conviction by 16 senator-judges is needed. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Israel election results live: count of absentee ballots under way as coalition talks set to begin
articles.summary: With the final count unlikely to shift results significantly, experts say Gadi Eisenkot’s hopes of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu rest on his willingness to work with Palestinian…

blocks.text: Final ballots being tallied with results expected to show no clear winner
Hello and welcome to our continuing coverage of the Israeli election.

With 91% of votes now counted, the current results show prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc projected to receive 53 seats, with the grouping of his opponent Gadi Eisenkot on 48 and the Palestinian parties on track to receive a record 19 seats.

The final tally of absentee ballots is not expected to significantly shift the results, and with no grouping managing to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, Israel could be in for weeks of uncertainty, as both sides try to gather enough support to form a government.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s bloc, has told Israeli media that he will meet leaders on Thursday for coalition talks. According to the Times of Israel, he will hold talks with Eisenkot, the leading opposition candidate and chair of the Yashar party, and Yair Lapid, the number-two in the opposition B’Yachad party.
This would mark the official start of coalition talks, and Golan has been the only opposition leader so far backing working with the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel.

blocks.caption: Leftwing protesters blocked roads in Tel Aviv on Wednesday evening to demand a joint government of Palestinians and Jewish Israelis. Photograph: Mostafa Alkharouf/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, voiced hope that the country could avoid a second election. “We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” said Herzog, who is tasked with determining which candidate to tap to form a government, urging parties to keep “an open mind”.

items: Israel’s future hangs in the balance after it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s historic elections. Indeed, Gadi Eisenkot and his allies face a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.

Yousef Jabareen, head of the Arab-majority Joint List, said the Israeli public had voted for new leadership and “anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu’s blood-soaked government will have to talk to us”. He told AFP that while he was willing to cooperate with an opposition-led government to unseat Netanyahu, he was not open to joining such a coalition outright. The ad hoc support of Palestinian lawmakers could enable Eisenkot to maintain a minority government, although few observers believe such an arrangement would survive for long.

Israel’s Central Elections Committee said it had received a Likud party complaint alleging that Arab parties had compromised election integrity and would examine the claims as part of its routine post-election review. Netanyahu’s party responded to partial election results showing Arab-led parties could play a king-making role in forming a new government by accusing them – without evidence – of “stealing” the election and demanding that the police and Shin Bet security service investigate the allegations.

UN rights chief Volker Turk has said that he hopes the next Israeli government will “change course massively” and respect international law. “The message is: don’t continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that’s what we have frankly seen in the current environment,” Turk told reporters in New York. He added: “Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them, and I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively.”

blocks.text: Israel’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalition

blocks.caption: Emma Graham-Harrison

blocks.text: Emma Graham-Harrison
Hours before the final results from Israel’s elections were in, several things were clear. Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition had lost its mandate, and the opposition had a firm majority.

But most of Israel’s Jewish opposition ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties, in the course of a racist election campaign in which Netanyahu painted Palestinian citizens as an enemy inside the state.

The self-imposed ban on a broader opposition alliance, if it holds, offers Netanyahu the prospect of turning his defeat into another term in office – or at least a prolonged mandate as caretaker prime minister and perhaps another round of elections.

This confected barrier to unseating Netanyahu became the focus of Israeli media and analysts. “No Clear Government” announced the newspaper Israel Hayom. “Road to Unity Government Has Been Paved”, read an article on Channel 12.

blocks.caption: Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra’am party, holds his daughter as he casts his vote in Maghar, Israel. Photograph: Rami Shlush/Reuters

blocks.text: Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, attacked that framing. “Netanyahu lost. I know how to count,” he said in a statement calling for a government with Palestinians, who make up about 20% of Israel’s population.

“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said. “We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Arab citizens of Israel.”
While Palestinian-led parties do not describe themselves as Zionist, neither do some of the ultra-Orthodox groups who are a key part of Netanyahu’s current coalition.

A survey taken as polls closed on election day showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with the Palestinian-led Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu, political psychology researcher Eran Halperin said.
But opposition leaders were silent on Wednesday, as they apparently tried to balance their desire to unseat Netanyahu with promises against working with Palestinians.

Former general Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the biggest opposition party, has not directly ruled out governing with Palestinians but laid out conditions that made it politically impossible for them to join a coalition.

Palestinians have been clearer about their priorities. “We are ready and prepared to pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government,” Yousef Jabareen, leader of the larger Joint List, said on Wednesday. “The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership.”

Israel’s elections committee has said it began counting absentee ballots at 1am local time. That count is expected to last until Thursday evening, with an estimated 500,000 ballots from military personnel and diplomats to be tallied up.
They are not expected to significantly change the results.

blocks.caption: A voter casts his ballot at a school used as a polling station during Israel’s general election in Tel Aviv. Photograph: David Goldman/AP

blocks.text: Under Israeli electoral law, each voter is assigned a specific polling station and can only vote at that station. However in exceptional circumstances, some voters are allowed to cast their ballot at special polling stations they are not registered at. Among those afforded this exception are soldiers stationed at IDF bases, diplomats working abroad, prisoners and prison guards and people in hospital.
These absentee ballots are transported directly to the Knesset where they undergo a series of checks before they are counted, which is why they arrive in the final count much later.

items: Israel’s future hangs in the balance after it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s historic elections. Indeed, Gadi Eisenkot and his allies face a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.

Yousef Jabareen, head of the Arab-majority Joint List, said the Israeli public had voted for new leadership and “anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu’s blood-soaked government will have to talk to us”. He told AFP that while he was willing to cooperate with an opposition-led government to unseat Netanyahu, he was not open to joining such a coalition outright. The ad hoc support of Palestinian lawmakers could enable Eisenkot to maintain a minority government, although few observers believe such an arrangement would survive for long.

Israel’s Central Elections Committee said it had received a Likud party complaint alleging that Arab parties had compromised election integrity and would examine the claims as part of its routine post-election review. Netanyahu’s party responded to partial election results showing Arab-led parties could play a king-making role in forming a new government by accusing them – without evidence – of “stealing” the election and demanding that the police and Shin Bet security service investigate the allegations.

UN rights chief Volker Turk has said that he hopes the next Israeli government will “change course massively” and respect international law. “The message is: don’t continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that’s what we have frankly seen in the current environment,” Turk told reporters in New York. He added: “Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them, and I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively.”

articles.title: China stocks slip as tech weakness overshadows Fed rate decision
articles.summary: 'We are wary that investor sentiment on AI is fragile; however, we believe the risk-reward is looking more attractive again, and interest may come back towards the end of the year as investors…

blocks.text: SHANGHAI, China – China stocks slipped on Thursday, October 29, as a deepening selloff in tech shares overshadowed the Federal Reserve’s decision to keep interest rates unchanged.
At the midday break, the benchmark Shanghai Composite index lost 0.9%, while the blue-chip CSI300 index .CSI300 fell 1.2%.
Tech shares were among the main drags, with the start-up board ChiNext Composite index falling 3.6% and Shanghai’s tech-focused STAR50 index tumbling 4.2%.
CSI 5G communications, a gauge that measures the industry, plunged 6.1% in morning deals.
Robot maker Yushu Technology, also known as Unitree, slumped 4.3% after its third-quarter net profit fell despite revenue rising 70% from a year earlier in its first earnings report since listing.

“Valuations for the tech AI hardware names are now close to the historical trough and imply a major deceleration in EPS growth ahead,” said James Wang, head of China strategy at UBS Investment Bank Research.

“We are wary that investor sentiment on AI is fragile; however, we believe the risk-reward is looking more attractive again, and interest may come back towards the end of the year as investors rebuild their portfolios for the new year.”
Across the region, Asian shares gave up earlier gains as AI-related earnings announcements prompted wildly mixed responses, raising the stakes for Amazon and Intel results due later in the day.

The Fed held interest rates steady, as expected, on Wednesday, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week’s US midterm elections while it awaits further data on inflation, which the central bank said “remains elevated.”
In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng index inched up 0.1%, while the city’s tech shares fell 2%.

articles.title: ‘The more you earn, the less you keep’: readers react to the budget
articles.summary: From a young chef and a single father to business owners and a pensioner, Guardian readers reveal how John Healey’s measures will affect them

blocks.text: ‘Most people my age have written off buying a home’
Louie, 24, a chef living in London, says a lot of people have “written off the idea of even considering getting a property” in their 20s.
He is optimistic about the government’s new Your First Home scheme, which will enable people to buy a new-build property with a deposit of just 2.5%, supported by an interest-free equity loan.
But he says a smaller deposit alone will not be enough for him. “I’ve found hospitality wages to be far too volatile to even consider saving for a property,” he says.

As a result, he is studying an access course with plans to start a physiotherapy degree next year. He hopes that by the time he graduates and gains some experience, he will have a stable enough income and sufficient savings to put down a deposit.

He says the new scheme “should encourage a lot of young people to buy earlier” and adds: “We are moving in a good direction, but I’ll still save and wait until around late 20s to early 30s to start [thinking about buying], just due to how much it may cost me.”

Louie earns between £37,000 and £40,000 a year and shares a three-bedroom rented property with two friends. But rent and bills take up an increasingly large proportion of his income, leaving little room to save towards buying a home.
“I was always told that a third of your salary should go towards rent and bills, but it’s coming up to about half now, which is a little bit mental,” he says.
His landlord recently informed the household that their rent would increase by £200 a month in November.

He has managed to build up some savings. Since he was 18, he has put between 5% and 10% of his earnings into a stocks and shares investment account, and over the past year has also started making regular contributions to an Isa specifically for a house deposit.
“Nobody really wants to be spending all their money on rent,” he says. “But with the amount of money we make, you kind of have to. ”
‘I earned £126,000 last year – but still have nothing at the end of the month’

blocks.caption: Graham earned £126,000 last year but says he has virtually nothing left in the bank each month. Photograph: Graham Robinson

blocks.text: Graham Robinson is a business owner from Timperley, Greater Manchester, who runs the company KeySim. He earned £126,000 last year, but says that despite his six-figure income, he has virtually nothing left in his bank account at the end of each month.
Graham says he was “hoping for real help with the cost of employing people” from the budget. “Instead, the employment allowance stays at £10,500, while employers pick up the rising wage bill.”
He adds: “The minimum wage increase is welcome for workers, but the government gets the headline, businesses get the bill and the Treasury recoups some through tax and national insurance.”
The 45-year-old lives alone and shares care of his 10-year-old autistic son with his ex, covering all childcare costs himself.

“I know £126,000 sounds like an enormous amount of money, but after tax it works out at broadly £6,500 a month, and that really doesn’t go as far as people might think,” he says. “I don’t have expensive cars, I don’t go on extravagant holidays. I don’t really do anything particularly lavish, but at the end of the month it’s all gone.”
His mortgage payments have risen from about £900 a month to £1,300, while council tax, food, energy and other everyday expenses have also increased.
Normally earning approximately £100,000 a year, he has increasingly relied on additional dividends from his business to cover rising costs.
He is frustrated by the effective 60% income tax rate on earnings caused by the gradual withdrawal of the personal allowance on income over £100,000, which reaches zero when earnings reach £125,140.
“To put an extra £1,000 a month in my take-home pay, my salary would need to rise from £100,000 to £129,757 a year,” he says.
‘Our mortgage has increased by more than £600 a month’

blocks.caption: Helen welcomes the £100 winter payment for households like hers, but questions the methodology. Photograph: Jonathan Clements

blocks.text: Helen, 40, lives in south-west London with her husband and two children, aged eight and five. She is the main breadwinner, working in communications, while her husband runs his own architectural practice.

Her house is in council tax band D, which means she will get a £100 energy payment this winter. She welcomed the extra money, but found the way it was being distributed strange, based on bands rather than financial need.

She says the change offering self-employed people paternity pay was “great”, though now her children are older it would not benefit her family. She adds: “It was lovely to hear Dolly Parton’s book scheme mentioned, as encouraging education for all is key.”
Her family’s biggest monthly expense is their mortgage, which increased by more than £600 a month when interest rates rose. They have now fixed it until 2028.

Helen says frozen income tax thresholds are one of her biggest concerns, alongside getting the economy growing and the pressures facing small businesses. Her husband’s architectural practice is less than four years old and has struggled with the rising costs of building and a wider slowdown in construction.
“The challenge comes down to the price of energy; for example, the cost of steel, transporting materials and building homes,” she says. “It impacts everything we make, build and buy.”
‘I don’t know how people live on just the state pension’

blocks.caption: Peter thinks pensioners should pay tax if they can and backs changes to the triple lock. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

blocks.text: Peter Pillinger, 72, is a widower from South Ribble in Lancashire whose state pension makes up about half his income. He also receives a pension from his career as a Methodist minister, a small amount from his late wife’s pension and an allowance for his work as a local councillor.
He is pleased with one of the key announcements: the scrapping of standing charges on gas bills. These are fixed daily fees that households pay regardless of how much gas they use.

“My gas bill in the summer is almost entirely standing charge,” he says. “They are regressive. Putting all the costs in the unit charge will encourage people to reduce usage and to insulate their homes.”
But he wonders why it will take until at least next spring for the change to come in. He also wants to know what the government will do “for those who need higher usage for medical reasons”.

He supports the changes to the state pension triple lock and believes pensioners who can afford to pay tax should do so. “If my income is £25,000 or approaching £30,000, why should it not be taxed? If everyone else is paying tax at that level, why should I not?”
Conversely, he is concerned about those surviving on much less. “I don’t know how people live on just the state pension,” he says.
‘Flowers are one of the first things people think to cut back on’

blocks.caption: Danielle says fuel costs are affecting the price of the flowers she buys and the expense of delivering them. Photograph: Danielle

blocks.text: Danielle Walker, 37, is a self-employed florist based in Wakefield, West Yorkshire. She says rising fuel prices are squeezing her business from both sides, increasing the cost of making deliveries while also pushing up the price of the flowers she buys.
She welcomes the chancellor cancelling the planned fuel duty rise, but adds “it doesn’t undo the increases we’ve already faced or take away the pressure we’re under”.
Increasing the higher mileage rate from 25p to 35p a mile will not benefit her, she says, nor will the business rate threshold going up from £12,000 to £18,000, as she works from a studio.

Danielle has spent considerable time calculating delivery charges for different postcodes to ensure they cover her fuel costs and the time spent travelling. But she says she is increasingly having to absorb some of these costs herself.

“If I’ve quoted flowers for a wedding based on diesel being £1.40 a litre and it’s £2 by the time the wedding comes around, I’ve still got to get there. There’s only so much you can absorb for so long,” she says.
With customers already struggling financially, she feels unable to keep passing on rising costs without risking a loss of business.
“Flowers are a luxury item, and when people are feeling the pinch, they’re one of the first things people think to cut back on,” she says.
Danielle believes the government should look at the impact of fuel duty and VAT on small businesses that depend on driving, arguing that independent traders are particularly exposed to rising prices.

“Someone has to take it on the chin somewhere. I feel it’s unfair that small businesses are continually having to absorb these costs or lose customers by being honest about what delivery should cost.”
‘I am a single dad. The more you earn, the less you keep’

Jonny Roberts, 39, is a single dad from Newbury, Berkshire, with children aged 11 and eight. He works part-time at McDonald’s and as a tutor, while also studying for an online master’s degree. Between his two jobs, he works the equivalent of full-time hours. But even with support from universal credit, his income only just covers essentials.

“We had heard in the run-up [to the budget] there would be something on energy bills, and I’m sure millions of households are grateful for the extra £100 help towards that announced today,” he says. “But it was disappointing to see no announcement on whether local housing allowance [LHA] will be uprated.”

For Jonny, one of the biggest problems is the gap between the housing support available through universal credit and the reality of renting. He is entitled to the three-bedroom LHA rate, which gives him £1,200 a month towards his rent, but he pays £1,300 a month for a two-bedroom flat.
“The rent we’re paying isn’t particularly high for the area. It’s pretty much in line with the norm,” he says.
“Last year’s freeze and the cuts of prior government mean the housing element of universal credit seems to live in an alternate reality to the actual rents charged in the south of England.”
Jonny is also frustrated by the way universal credit reduces the financial rewards of taking on additional work.

For every extra pound he earns above his work allowance, his universal credit is reduced by 55p. Once income tax, national insurance and student loan repayments are taken into account, he says the amount he keeps from an additional shift can be surprisingly small.

With rent taking up the largest share of his budget, Jonny has little flexibility when other household costs rise. “I’m happy to go with less for myself to make sure I can feed all three of us,” he says.
Jonny was happy to see a “speeding up of the rollout of free breakfast clubs to an extra 2,000 schools” but adds: “It still seems a glacial pace when there are 17,000 primaries in the country.”

items: Jonny takes part in Changing Realities, a collaboration involving more than 200 parents and carers living on low incomes, researchers at the University of Glasgow and Child Poverty Action Group. The project documents families’ experiences of living on a low income and brings their voices into discussions about poverty and social security policy.

articles.title: How will John Healey’s energy support package affect you?
articles.summary:
Chancellor’s ‘new course’ includes a £100 one-off payment, low-carbon upgrade loans and an end to standing charges

John Healey has unveiled a package of support for households being buffeted…

blocks.text: John Healey has unveiled a package of support for households being buffeted by “global economic storms”.

“I’m setting a new course to get energy costs down in line with Europe,” the chancellor said in his maiden budget. In the long term, he hopes that changes in how Britain covers the cost of renewables and grid upgrades will “drive down all aspects of energy bills”.
British households face some of the highest energy charges for three years, with the war in the Middle East driving up oil and gas prices.
Under the government’s price cap, average dual-fuel bills are £1,700 a year and could rise to more than £2,100 a year from January, according to industry forecasts.
So what has the chancellor offered hard-pressed households to help them through the coldest months of the year? And will it be enough to lower gas and electricity bills?

blocks.caption: Removing standing charges from gas bills will help two-thirds of households save an average of £45 a year.  Photograph: Paul Melling/Alamy

blocks.text: The £100 ‘household energy payment’

The government’s biggest bet on offering “breathing space” to struggling households this winter is a one-off payment of £100 in January for 20m households in council tax bands A to D. It is also the measure most likely to deliver real benefit for those in need.
The £2.6bn “household energy payment” will go directly into bank accounts to “take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people through to the spring”, according to Healey.
Martin Lewis, the founder of MoneySavingExpert.com, said households could face a 25% cost increase from January and shouldn’t expect to feel better off than they do today.

Officials are anxious to avoid handing public money to those who can get by without it but they lack household income data to target proposed support. Using council tax bands is “the least worst proxy”, Lewis said.
The payment will be in addition to the Warm Home Discount, which offers about 6m means-tested households in England, Wales and Scotland £150 off winter fuel bills.
An end to gas standing charges
This measure will offer a modest saving for most British households – but not all, and perhaps not until next winter.

Healey promised to end “unfair and outdated” standing charges on gas bills for 23m homes “in 2027 or as soon as possible after”. This could help almost two-thirds of households to save an average of £45 a year.

A standing charge is a fixed daily fee paid through all household gas bills, regardless of how much is used. It means homes that severely ration their gas use – or use none at all – still shoulder the same cost as a high-income household.

The charge typically adds about £100 a year to bills and the change means these costs will soon be recovered through a higher unit price for gas. For those with below-average gas use, bills should fall. But there won’t be savings for everyone.

Jonny Marshall, an economist at the Resolution Foundation, said households with high gas use might have higher bills when the unit rate increases. These could include low-income households who have bigger families or poorly insulated homes.

A home using 7,000 kilowatt hours of gas a year would save about £40 under the change, but a household using 14,000 kWh of gas a year could be £25 worse off, according to Richard Neudegg, a director at Uswitch.com. A household using the typical 11,500 kWh shouldn’t see any change, he added.
Lower electricity levies
The government has already begun taking aim at taxes and policy costs loaded on to electricity bills that could over time mean removing hundreds of pounds from bills.
This month, it removed the 5% VAT levy on electricity bills for 29m households, effectively saving them about £45 a year.

This was supposed to help households through the coldest months of the year, until March. But Healey has promised to keep VAT off bills until July, extending the annual savings to £50 a year, according to the Treasury.
The move follows a string of cuts to electricity levies over the past year which have shaved about £150 a year off costs.

“For many years, under Conservative governments, policy costs were simply loaded on to household bills through levies,” Healey said. “Today, I am putting an end to that. We’ll introduce a new cost control framework to drive down all aspects of energy bills.”

Healey confirmed he would consider steps to remove standing charges on electricity too, which ​add about £200 a year to the average ​bill. The savings from this measure remain unclear, depending on which costs would move into general taxation and which would be covered through the unit price for electricity.

Healey will continue to alter a subsidy scheme for the UK’s oldest renewable energy projects, around three-quarters of which has been removed from bills and covered by general taxation. The research charity Nesta said this would lower electricity costs by £42 a year.
Healey has scrapped plans for a levy to support hydrogen projects that would otherwise have added £2.60 to £4.50 a year to the average dual-fuel bill.
Low-carbon home upgrades

The government believes that households could save up to £550 a year on energy bills if they invest in solar panels, home batteries and a heat pump. These savings could rise by a further £300 a year with a time-of-use tariff, according to the government.
To help households access these savings, a Warm Home Loans scheme, which launched on Tuesday, will offer government-backed loans of up to £35,000 for low-carbon energy alternatives.
The government said it was committed to rolling out heat pumps through its boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants of up to £7,500 to help meet the £13,600 cost of installing one.
Grants of up to £9,000 a year are available to households that are not connected to the gas grid and rely on high-cost heating oil.
Energy debt relief
For many, the government’s new measures will come too late to help this winter. But there could be support in the spring from a debt relief scheme.

The government said the delayed scheme will “provide targeted support to customers in genuine financial need”. Total household energy debt has tripled from 2021 to a record £5bn and could reach £7bn by the end of the year.
The one-off, targeted intervention has been designed to help those with debts from the 2022-24 energy crisis and little prospect of repaying them.
Nesta has suggested debt relief could be given to about 2m households for a one-off cost of £2.7bn. This would also cut the £29 a year paid by all households to cover the cost of unpaid bills.
More details on the scheme will follow in early 2027, the government said.

articles.title: Thames Water creditors to vote on emergency £2.4bn loan as cash runs low
articles.summary:
Campaigners say costly new funds will lead to higher bills, which company denies

A group of creditors to troubled Thames Water are poised to vote on whether to grant an emergency £2.4bn loan…

blocks.text: A group of creditors to troubled Thames Water are poised to vote on whether to grant an emergency £2.4bn loan to keep the company afloat, as campaigners raise concerns it could add £40 to each household’s bills in interest alone.

A consortium of creditors, called London & Valley Water, will vote on Thursday on whether to increase a funding facility for the debt-laden utility company to £5.4bn to keep it operating to autumn 2027.
The company’s class A creditors, which include BlackRock, Elliott Management and Silver Point Capital, last year granted it a £3bn loan at a 9.75% interest rate.

This month, Thames Water said it needed a further £2.4bn cash injection because it would be unable to reach a longer-term deal to sort out its extensive debt pile before running out of cash by “the end of 2026 or the start of 2027”.
Thames Water has previously said that customers will not be on the hook for the interest on the £3bn loan, but it has almost run out of money and not paid down the debt.

Analysis by the campaign group We Own It showed that the £2.4bn loan, if it is granted on the same terms and added to bills, would cost £40 per household in interest alone, and £454 per household if the entire loan amount was included. London & Valley Water insisted it would not be added to bills.

Andy Burnham is now deciding whether to allow a takeover deal by the water company’s creditors, which would entail writing off fines and reducing environmental commitments. He is also mulling whether to nationalise the company or take another form of state control.

blocks.caption: The Liberal Democrat MP Charlie Maynard is among those calling for Thames Water to be put into special administration.  Photograph: Laurie Noble

blocks.text: Some Labour politicians and environmental campaigners have said Burnham should instead put Thames Water into special administration, a form of temporary government control while a new buyer is sought.

Sophie Conquest, the lead campaigner at We Own It, said: “Since privatisation, £11.9bn has been extracted from Thames Water. They have already had more than enough of our money. If they cannot survive without yet another excruciatingly expensive bailout, this government must let them go bust and bring them into special administration, followed by permanent public ownership.”

The utility company serves 16 million customers in London and the Thames Valley. It has been on the brink of collapse for several years after it became overwhelmed by a debt pile that is now about £20bn. Its shareholders walked away in 2024, leaving the company under the effective control of its creditors while they work out a deal to avoid bankruptcy.
In 2025, Charlie Maynard, the Liberal Democrat MP for Witney, along with campaigners and junior creditors, unsuccessfully took the water company to court over the £3bn loan.
On the proposed £2.4bn loan, he said: “The creditors will likely hand Thames Water yet another massively overpriced rescue loan, which customers will end up having to pay for.

“This is just another short-term fix, paid for by customers and taxpayers. The government has had more than two years to make up its mind. It’s time it did so. Put Thames Water into special administration now.”
The creditors have approved 15 previous consent requests from Thames Water. The company said this month it had so far drawn £2.65bn of the £3bn available under the “super senior” facility.
after newsletter promotion

Prof Dieter Helm, an economist at the University of Oxford, doubted that a turnaround of Thames Water could be “properly funded” and said further loans were merely postponing an “inevitable” special administration.

He said: “The future investment programme for the turnaround will not be properly funded. Thames – and indeed much of the rest of the industry – is caught between a political rock and a political hard place.”
Conquest added: “During a cost of living crisis, this government cannot continue to reward Thames Water’s failures at our expense.”

Burnham has been looking at ways to take control of Thames Water in an early test of his promise to bring “the essentials of life” under public control. He has urged his advisers to go back to the drawing board and create a list of policies for the utility company.
One option under consideration is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines into a government stake in the company, saving its creditors money but giving ministers some say in how it is run.

A Thames Water spokesperson said: “Additional liquidity from creditors will enable the investment to continue uninterrupted while the business seeks a recapitalisation. Customer bills are set by Ofwat, and this funding does not add any costs for households.”

A spokesperson for the London & Valley Water consortium said: “No customer bills will be used to pay for the costs of Thames Water’s rescue financing. These costs are borne entirely by the class A creditors.

“Creditors have stepped in to provide the billions of pounds of private capital needed to ensure Thames Water’s record infrastructure investment programme can continue, avoiding the need for any government financial support or taxpayer funding.”

articles.title: Truck helper dies, driver hurt in Quezon road collision
articles.summary: LUCENA CITY — A 42-year-old truck helper died while the driver was injured when their vehicle collided with an Isuzu refrigerated van on Wednesday night in Atimonan, Quezon. The truck was negotiating…

articles.title: North Korea fires around 10 ballistic missiles into sea
articles.summary: The latest ballistic missile launch comes amid rising border tensions with South Korea and uncertainty over potential nuclear talks with the US.

image.caption: South Korean television reports on North Korea's latest missile test on October 12, 2026 in SeoulImage: Ahn Young-joon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast on Thursday, South Korea's military said.
The missiles were launched at around 12:30 p.m. local time (0330 GMT) from an area near Wonsan on North Korea's eastern coast, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a statement.
South Korea's military said it was strengthening surveillance and maintaining readiness for additional launches while closely sharing information with the United States and Japan.
Japan's Defense Ministry said the missiles had fallen outside the country's Exclusive Economic Zone, according to South Korea's Yonhap News Agency.
Pyongyang has conducted missile tests on more than 10 occasions this year, most recently launching several short-range ballistic missiles on October 12.
Thursday's launch comes amid growing tensions between the two Koreas over a border dispute that has further strained relations between Seoul and Pyongyang.
Why are tensions rising between North and South Korea?
Three South Korean soldiers were wounded on September 21 when landmines exploded in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), which separates the two countries.
A joint investigation by South Korea and the United Nations concluded earlier this month that North Korea had planted the landmines south of the military demarcation line more than a year ago.
Pyongyang has denied responsibility and warned of retaliation if provoked.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, condemned South Korean demands for an apology as "despicable." She also rejected Seoul's offer of medical equipment.

blocks.caption: Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, has rejected South Korean demands for an apology over a landmine explosion [FILE: August 10, 2022]Image: Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Last week, North Korea announced plans to resume propaganda broadcasts along the border and deploy new weapons systems in the area.
South Korea subsequently proposed talks to clarify the border and prevent accidental military clashes. Pyongyang has yet to respond.
What about potential US-North Korea nuclear talks?
The rising tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that South Korea could be sidelined in potential nuclear negotiations.

blocks.caption: US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un met at the demarcation line between North and South Korea during Trump's first term in 2019 [FILE: June 30, 2019]Image: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: Seoul is a key Washington ally, but Trump's approach has fueled uncertainty over South Korea's role in any future talks with the North.
North Korea's previous missile launch on October 12 came a day after Trump suggested he might meet Kim Jong Un this year.

articles.title: LTO vows lawful license revocation for drunk drivers
articles.summary: The Land Transportation Office (LTO) on Thursday vowed proper implementation of license revocation for drivers caught driving under the influence of alcohol.

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 12:51pm
The Land Transportation Office (LTO) on Thursday vowed proper implementation of license revocation for drivers caught driving under the influence of alcohol.

“Gusto nating matiyak na walang driver na makapagmaneho nang lasing o nasa impluwensiya ng droga nang hindi napapanagot sa batas. Pero mahalaga ring tama ang proseso ng panghuhuli dahil ang pagpapatupad ng batas ay dapat mahigpit, maayos, at walang pagkukulang,” said LTO Chief Assistant Secretary Markus Lacanilao.

(We want to guarantee that there will be no driver who will drive drunk or under the influence of drugs that will not be held accountable to the law. But it is important that we follow the proper processes of apprehension because the implementation of the law should be strict, orderly, and no lapses.)

The LTO previously said that it would start revoking the licenses of drunk drivers beginning November 15. With the issuance of Memorandum No. MVL-2026-242, law enforcement officers are told to strictly follow the guidelines.

“Inatasan ang mga law enforcement officers na sundin ang tamang pagkakasunod-sunod ng pagsusuri bago hulihin ang isang driver na pinaghihinalaang nagmamaneho sa ilalim ng impluwensiya ng alak,” the LTO said in a Facebook post.
(Law enforcement officers are told to follow the proper order of testing before a driver suspected of driving under the influence of alcohol is detained.)

Should the driver fail the Field Sobriety Test, then the officer will use a breath analyzer to measure the amount of alcohol in the driver’s system. The breathalyzer will not be the only test, the LTO clarified.

Other than the possible penalties of violating the Anti-Drunk and Drugged Driving Act, the LTO chief is given the power under the Land Transportation and Traffic Code to revoke the license of someone deemed by the LTO Law Enforcement Service (LES) as an “Improper Person to Operate a Motor Vehicle.”
The LES will then submit to the Investigation Division (IID) the record of every apprehension, including cases where the driver would refuse to be tested for proper action. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Hey hun’: police colleague messaged Beau Lamarre-Condon on Instagram after alleged murders, court hears
articles.summary:
Trial also hears accused told police he wasn’t ‘avoiding them’ in three-minute call before he turned himself in after allegedly murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies

A police officer accused…

blocks.text: A police officer accused of a double murder told police he was not avoiding them despite vanishing for days after the incident, a Sydney court has heard.

The court heard police attempted to contact Beau Lamarre-Condon after the alleged murders, with a colleague messaging him on Instagram: “Hey hun ... can you please contact the crime manager at eastern suburbs asap when you get a chance?”
Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to murdering his ex partner Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in an inner-city terrace on 19 February 2024.
Police tried unsuccessfully to contact him for four days before he turned himself in, the court heard.
He then led officers to a rural property where the bodies of both men, who were aged in their 20s, were found in surfboard bags.
“I just either want to let a detective or a sergeant know I am not avoiding them,” the 31-year-old said during a three-minute phone call to police on 22 February.
“Just tell them I will come in tomorrow.”
The evidence was heard during a New South Wales supreme court jury trial on Thursday as prosecutors read a statement by the officer who took the call.
The morning before the alleged murders, Lamarre-Condon messaged a friend – known by the pseudonym Fiona Rosso – not to worry about him and that he would call later.
“Also I’ve just gotten rid of all social media,” he wrote.
He turned up to Rosso’s home three days after the alleged murders crying and saying he had “done something bad”, the jury heard on Wednesday.
Lamarre-Condon told her police had tried to contact him but he put his phone on aeroplane mode.
Armed with two buckets, he scrubbed blood from the back of a white van parked outside Rosso’s home, the jury heard.
He then spent the night there before driving to Sydney.
Rosso testified Lamarre-Condon’s mother texted him the code word “hot chocolate”, meaning police had searched her home after the alleged murders.
A statement by Const Hayley Keefe was read on Thursday outlining attempts by NSW police to contact her colleague and friend.
She was asked by a crime manager to contact Lamarre-Condon on his personal Instagram account.
On 21 February, she followed through.
“Hey hun ... can you please contact the crime manager at eastern suburbs asap when you get a chance?” she wrote.
The message remained unread and she deleted it, feeling awkward for using her personal social media for business, she wrote in her statement.
The crown alleges Lamarre-Condon killed Baird “execution-style” at close range through a plan borne of a jealous obsession, before shooting Davies to eliminate a witness.
The 31-year-old claims he acted in self-defence after entering the terrace to retrieve his belongings.
His offer to plead guilty to Baird’s manslaughter was rejected by prosecutors.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: Outcry after Call of Duty maker uses real footage of deadly Seoul crowd crush in new video game
articles.summary:
Bereaved families have urged the publisher of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to remove a clip from the game that shows a figure performing CPR and bodies lying in the street

Bereaved…

blocks.text: Bereaved families in South Korea have demanded that the makers of Call of Duty remove harrowing footage of the deadly 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the latest instalment of the video game.

The clips, which are seconds-long, appear in the opening moments of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and are used to represent a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional North Korean invasion.
One shows a scene of chaos with a figure performing CPR on a victim lying in the street. Another shows rows of bodies laid out in the road, and a victim being carried away on a stretcher.

A total of 158 people were killed in a narrow alley in Seoul’s Itaewon nightlife district during the Halloween weekend in 2022. Two more have since been recognised as victims, having died from trauma caused by the disaster.

“We are appalled that the chaotic and desperate scenes, in which countless citizens performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the cold street, were used exactly as they were to create a scene in a game,” the bereaved families’ council and a coalition of civic groups said in a joint statement on Wednesday, demanding that the footage be removed.

They said people who had taken part in the rescue or witnessed the crush were still living with trauma, while hateful comments about the victims were spreading online in connection with the game’s premise.

blocks.caption: A screengrab from the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 game released by Activision, which is made up of real news broadcast footage from Getty showing paramedics performing CPR during the 2022 Itaewon crowd crush. Composite: Youtube/Activision

blocks.text: Activision, the game’s publisher, told the Yonhap news agency that “some actual news footage included in the game’s opening cinematic was utilised as an element to convey the fictional story within the work.”
They added, “We had absolutely no intention of mentioning or treating lightly any actual tragic events, including the Itaewon tragedy.”
The Guardian has contacted Activision for comment.
The demand comes as the country marks the fourth anniversary of the crush on Thursday.
Players in South Korea identified the clip after the game’s release, and Korean broadcasters have compared it side by side with footage filmed on the night of the crowd crush.
The Korean Game Users Association called for an apology and for the footage to be replaced.
Modern Warfare 4 follows a South Korean marine private fighting a North Korean invasion through recognisable Korean streets.

The title had already become a political talking point before its release, with conservative politicians urging president Lee Jae Myung – who is pursuing a more conciliatory approach towards North Korea – to play the game to understand what they described as the threat from Pyongyang.
It topped South Korea’s sales chart on Steam, the leading PC gaming platform, within days of its release.

articles.title: Bernardo says Martin Romualdez did not ask him for DPWH projects, kickbacks
articles.summary: State witness and former Public Works undersecretary Roberto Bernardo on Thursday said that Leyte Rep. Ferdinand Martin Romualdez did not ask him for a list of infrastructure projects in exchange of…

blocks.text: FLOOD CONTROL MESS
Published October 29, 2026 12:38pm

State witness and former Public Works undersecretary Roberto Bernardo on Thursday said that Leyte Rep. Ferdinand Martin Romualdez did not ask him for a list of infrastructure projects in exchange of commitments or kickbacks.

Bernardo made the testimony during the hearing on the bail petition of Romualdez amid a P7.4 billion plunder leveled against the latter alongside former House appropriations panel chairperson Zaldy Co, personal assistant Joselyn Tragua Sereño, and Felicito Cristobal Guevarra, president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corporation.

During the cross-examination conducted by Romualdez’s lawyer, Bernardo confirmed that in his six affidavits and two judicial affidavits, he did not mention that the former House speaker asked him for projects or kickback.
Asked if he never referred to Romualdez as a proponent, Bernardo answered in the affirmative.
Asked if the lawmaker never requested for list of projects from him, Bernardo said, “Yes, Ma'am. Hindi po (He did not make a request)."
“Wala pong ganun (There is no such kind),” he added.
Bernardo was also asked if he is aware of any commitment or kickback delivered to Romualdez, Bernardo said, “Wala po (None).”
He then said he mentioned Romualdez in his affidavits in the context of seeing the former Speaker during the birthday celebration of then DPWH secretary Mark Villar in September 2016.
Bernardo also admitted that he had a financial gain of 1% for every transaction involving then DPWH Bulacan First District Engineering Office District Engineer Henry Alcantara and Co.

He said that Alcantara and then DPWH National Capital Region director would provide the list of projects for proponent lawmakers for funding, and would also collect commitment fees from contractors since this will serve as kickback for proponents.
“Boss, hati na tayo sa (let's split the) 2%,” Bernardo recalled Alcantara as saying to him.
Asked by the Romualdez’s lawyer if he receives portion of the amount of a project cost, Bernardo replied, “in some cases.”
He, however, said he has no personal knowledge of the dealings between Alcantara and Co.
“Sinabi niya (Alcantara) [lang] po sa akin na nagdedeliver siya kay Zaldy Co (Alcantara told me he was making deliveries to Co),” Bernardo said.
The former DPWH undersecretary said Co only phoned him in 2021 to inquire about Alcantara.
“Sabi ko po maayos kausap si Alcantara (I vouched for Alcantara). Professional,” Bernardo said.
Turning a new leaf

Bernardo was also quizzed by Romualdez’s defense team on his statement in his judicial affidavit that he came forward about the flood control scheme because the people who have helped him before did not help him when he was grilled in the Senate inquiry on the flood control mess.
Bernardo, however, said that the people turning their backs on him was not the only reason for him to tell the truth.
“Hindi ko po masasabi na 'yun lang ang dahilan. When I learned about ghost projects, hindi ko na po kayang dalhin iyon. Kailangan matigil 'yun,” Bernardo said.
(I cannot say that people turning their backs on me was my only reason. It became such a burden for me when I learned about ghost projects. That should stop.) —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Business, advocacy groups call for removal of 'insertions' in proposed P7.2-T nat'l budget
articles.summary: Business and advocacy groups on Thursday called on Congress to remove alleged congressional insertions from the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 12:35pm
Business and advocacy groups on Thursday called on Congress to remove alleged congressional insertions from the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.

In a joint statement, 35 groups urged leaders of both chambers—Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, House Speaker Faustino Dy III, Senate Finance Committee Chair Joseph Victor Ejercito, and House Appropriations Committee Chair Mikaela Angela Suansing—to scrap "every congressional insertion that has no technical basis" from the proposed next year's budget.
Signatories in the joint statement are as follows:

blocks.text: "The House General Appropriations Bill (HB 10858), approved on third reading earlier this month by a vote of 281-13, added more than P180 billion in Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) allocations through the Budget Amendments and Review Subcommittee (BARSc)," the groups said.

"Independent budget watchdogs report that these additions cover at least 6,000 projects, raising the DPWH project count in the National Expenditure Program (NEP) to at least 16,000. Many appear as lump sums for multi-purpose buildings and access and bypass roads, without published project lists or named proponents," the groups added.

The joint statement was issued after the People's Budget Coalition (PBC) earlier said it found "red flags" amounting to over P1 trillion in allocations in the proposed P7.2 trillion national budget for fiscal year 2027.
These reportedly covered various types of "pork" or discretionary funds under the House-approved General Appropriations Bill (GAB).

"These additions were reportedly funded in part by cutting about P130 billion from foreign-assisted projects, P9.5 billion from calamity funds,P1.76 billion from the EDSA Busway, and P4.9 billion from health programs," the groups said.
"We find this deeply troubling."

The groups further said that foreign-assisted projects are the country's "most rigorously prepared infrastructure," which are backed by feasibility studies, financing commitments, and international procurement standards.

"Cutting them delays the high-impact projects that lower logistics costs and attract investments. Raiding calamity funds in a country that is exposed to disasters is indefensible. The Filipino people have already paid dearly for this practice. Insertions in the 2023 to 2025 budgets were linked to ghost and substandard flood control projects that betrayed public trust, wasted scarce resources, and left communities exposed to floods. The 2027 budget must not repeat that history," the groups said.

With this, the groups recommended to remove every insertion that lacks technical basis; restore the funds taken from foreign-assisted projects, calamity funds, EDSA Busway and health programs; strike special provisions that allow agencies to modify or replace projects; publish every amendment in full; and admit no new items at the Bicameral Conference Committee.
"The bicameral report must reconcile only what each chamber has already approved, contain no blank or lump-sum entries, and be deliberated in fully livestreamed sessions," the groups said.

"We welcome the commitments made by Senate President Gatchalian and Senator Ejercito that the Senate will scrutinize the House version line by line and will not accept last-minute insertions. We likewise acknowledge Speaker Dy's pledge of an open budget process. We ask both chambers to honor these commitments in full," the groups added.
Malacañang earlier defended budget insertions, saying these only become problematic if they go into politicians' pockets.

"Kung ang mga proyekto naman ng isang congressman ay maayos at ang pondong ilalaan dito ay magagamit nang tama, sino ba naman ang dapat na humadlang kung ang pondong ito ay sasapat naman para mapaganda ang isang distrito?" Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said.
(If a congressman's projects are justifiable and the allocated funds for such would be properly used to improve the district, then why should we stand in the way?)
— VDV, GMA News

articles.title: We shouldn’t ‘blindly’ believe allegations of violence against women, Queensland’s new DV minister said in resurfaced comments
articles.summary:
Concerns raised about appointment of former federal senator, Amanda Stoker, who has previously supported the rights of people accused of sexual assault

  • Get our

blocks.text: Women’s safety advocates have raised concerns about the appointment of rightwing Queensland MP Amanda Stoker as the state’s minister for the prevention of domestic violence in light of her resurfaced statements that people should not “blindly” believe women who make allegations of violence.

Stoker, who was appointed to the role on Saturday, argued in a 2023 article that the recent push to believe complaints “rather than carefully assess[ing] relevant evidence” would harm innocent defendants.
The former federal senator, has repeatedly supported the rights of people accused of sexual assault and implied some were subject to “false allegations”.
Former Australian of the year Grace Tame, who in 2021 criticised Stoker’s appointment to the federal outer ministry, said the appointment was “disappointing”.

Stoker’s appointment this week was welcomed in public by some in the community sector. Guardian Australia has also spoken to several people who work in Queensland supporting victims of domestic and sexual violence who said they had private concerns about Stoker taking over the portfolio, which includes responsibility for the child safety system, after the resignation of Amanda Camm.
None would speak publicly, in an environment where support organisations say they’ve been warned not to criticise the government, and others have had public funding cut.

Stoker made a public name for herself as a young conservative warrior, becoming a headline speaker at anti-abortion rallies who was chosen for the Senate in 2018 with the backing of the Liberal National party’s faction of “Christian soldiers”.
She left the Senate in 2022 and was elected to the Queensland parliament in 2024.

In a 2023 opinion piece published by independent thinktank, the Menzies Research Centre, Stoker raised concern about victim-focused reforms to the criminal justice system, including changes that allow the media to name accused rapists before they go to trial.

She said the changes removed “a small protection against the harm done to an accused’s reputation from adverse publicity in cases so weak that they don’t even meet the standard necessary to go to trial”.

“In our sincere desire to ensure that victims are treated with respect and dignity and are able to achieve justice, so-called ‘reforms’ have been proffered that would permanently undermine our justice system in a way that harms everyone,” Stoker wrote.

“What I do know is that the push for us all to blindly ‘#believeher’ (or any witness) rather than carefully assess the relevant evidence is prone to cause great harm to those defendants who are innocent.”

Stoker has repeatedly made comments over several years that suggest false allegations of sexual assault are made. She told Sky News in 2019, in relation to universities’ handling of sexual assault allegations: “we don’t want to see victims harmed, but we also don’t want to see people harmed by false allegations”.
Research has established that false allegations in sexual and domestic violence cases are rare.
The Queensland Police Service, on its website, says there is “no evidence that many women make vexatious reports” of sexual violence and that the rate of false allegations is “very low”.

“This myth about false allegations is harmful for society and harmful for victims of sexual offences,” the QPS says. “It contributes to under-reporting. And victims wrongly fear they will be met with disbelief and blame if they report.”
The CEO of Full Stop Australia, Karen Bevan, said “what leaders say about sexual violence is heard by every person deciding whether to tell someone what happened to them”.
“Victim-survivors need to know that if they come forward, they will be believed, supported and taken seriously,” Bevan said.
“In Queensland, 92% of women who experience sexual assault never report it to police.

“Believing someone when they disclose is not the same as deciding guilt. Police still investigate, and courts still test the evidence. A fair trial and a system that victim-survivors trust can, and must, exist together.”

Stoker’s office did not address specific questions sent on Tuesday, including whether her prior statements were consistent with the state government’s promise to put “victims at the heart of government”.
A spokesperson said there was broader context to the minister’s prior comments. They also said that the minister has a legal background and “cares deeply about procedural fairness in all cases”.

The spokesperson said the minister was “looking forward to engaging with, supporting, and hearing from all stakeholders and organisations within the new portfolio remit and supports the policy direction of the Crisafulli government, as she has consistently done since the government was elected”.
Stoker also did not respond to questions about whether she supported safeguarding measures to support victim-survivors, including the ability for some to give evidence from a “safe room”.

In her 2023 piece, Stoker wrote that removing “the right to face one’s accuser” or the ability to fully test evidence in court would “increase the number of innocent people who will be punished for crimes they didn’t commit”.
Tame said Stoker’s appointment was “very disappointing, considering that as we know that sexual, family and domestic violence in Australia is only worsening.
“Amanda has essentially played into the overarching gaslighting that is directed at victim survivors,” Tame said.

articles.title: Are GCash’s P10 transfer fees here to stay?
articles.summary: Talks with the central bank continue, says GCash

blocks.text: Talks with the central bank continue, says GCash
MANILA, Philippines – GCash isn’t committing to further reducing its P10 bank transfer fee just yet.

At a media briefing following its historic October 20 stock market debut, Rappler asked executives of GCash parent Mynt how the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) new transfer fees rules would affect its revenues and whether keeping the P10 charge could hurt its competitiveness.

Jep Tang, Mynt’s head of capital markets and investor relations, clarified that BSP Circular No. 1238 does not require banks and e-wallets to offer free transfers. Rather, it requires a more reasonable pricing structure, with charges reflecting the actual costs of providing the service.
“We have a good working relationship with the regulators, and this discussion is still ongoing as to what level it should be moving forward,” Tang said.
Pressed on whether GCash could lose customers to banks offering free transfers, Tang pointed to the company’s diversified revenue streams.

“Our top payments use cases, there are five, and these five use cases account for 78% of our payment solutions revenue. And bank transfer fee is not one of them,” he said. “So, definitely, because we’ve reduced from P15 to P10, clearly that has been reduced. But what we’d like to highlight, and what we really want to see is that there will be more use cases because of these changes.” (READ: After the IPO party, GCash comes for 5-6 lending next)
After the briefing, Rappler asked Tang about the status of discussions with the BSP. He stated that they were ongoing, although he declined to speculate on what the outcome of such talks could be.
BSP Deputy Governor for Payments and Currency Management Mamerto Tangonan also confirmed to Rappler that the central bank is still continuing negotiations with the e-wallet giant.
“We’re discussing,” Tangonan told Rappler on October 22, declining to give a timeline on when a resolution might be reached.

blocks.caption: BSP presses GCash, Maya on P10 transfer fees: Explain!

blocks.text: The financial stakes are difficult to pin down, even with GCash now a publicly listed company.

According to GCash’s IPO prospectus, four revenue-generating services, GLoad, GBills, Pay Online, and offline payments, accounted for 78% of its payment solutions revenue in the first half of 2026. Express Send, its fifth flagship service, allows users to transfer money between GCash accounts for free. These are considered on-us transfers, compared with off-us transfers to other banks and e-wallets, for which GCash charges P10.

These off-us transfers fall under the remaining 22%, alongside cash-in services, remittances, disbursements, merchant services, and other businesses. GCash does not disclose how much revenue comes specifically from the P10 transfer fee.
Interestingly, the prospectus also acknowledges that further fee reductions could hurt its business. (READ: Why exactly did BPI make transfers free?)

“Compliance with BSP Circular No. 1238 may require us to modify our pricing mechanisms, including with respect to transfer fees for certain electronic payment transactions, which could reduce Payment Solutions revenues. While reduced transfer fees may drive increased transaction volumes and broader user adoption of the GCash App, there can be no assurance that any such increase will fully offset the resulting reduction in per-transaction fee revenues,” Mynt said in its propsectus.

blocks.caption: Big IPO, big bonus: GCash employees get their own payday

blocks.text: Remember when Queen Máxima of the Netherlands visited the Philippines in 2024 as the United Nations’ special advocate for financial inclusion and asked a fisherman whether GCash was expensive?

He agreed, wishing there were no deductions from his transactions. The Dutch royal later met GCash CEO Martha Sazon at the company’s headquarters, although what they discussed remained behind closed doors.

After meeting the Queen, BSP Governor Eli Remolona Jr. likewise told reporters that he wanted to “know the cost structure” of digital payments and determine the right threshold for fee-free transactions.
Two years later, the BSP is still scrutinizing transfer fees charged by the country’s biggest e-wallets.
GCash and rival Maya both reduced their InstaPay fees from P15 to P10 in July, but stopped there. And while GCash is leaving its options open, Maya appears more inclined to keep charging.

In an earlier interview with Rappler, PLDT head of investor relations Jinggay Nograles described transfers as “one of the pillars of revenues” for Maya, which operates with a different cost structure from traditional banks.
“Maya needs to be a going concern,” Nograles said. “Looking at that particular revenue stream, it does make sense for Maya to keep that P10 fee.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Leak website releases data on thousands of US Homeland Security employees
articles.summary: The leaked data is on more than 40,000 Department of Homeland Security employees. DHS is aware of the potential breach and working to address it.

blocks.text: The leaked data is on more than 40,000 Department of Homeland Security employees. DHS is aware of the potential breach and working to address it.

items: Distributed Denial of Secrets released data on over 40,000 Department of Homeland Security employees, including sensitive information related to surveillance and human intelligence.
DHS acknowledged a potential breach and is working to protect its employees while addressing the situation, which is part of a series of recent government data leaks.

The leaked data includes personal information and job details of DHS employees, and a search tool has been developed to allow public access to the information, aiming to enhance accountability and oversight.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, USA – The leak website Distributed Denial of Secrets said on Wednesday, October 28, it has released data on more than 40,000 Department of Homeland Security employees, including details about officials working in sensitive fields such as surveillance and human intelligence.

DHS said in a statement it was “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.” The agency said it was working to ensure its employees were properly protected and would update the public “when more information is available.”

The disclosure — which the nonprofit data transparency group says draws on information obtained by an entity calling itself “Department of Peace” — is the third major government data leak to have made headlines in the past month.

In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees. Last week, the Defense Department was hit with a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel.

The DHS data includes names, phone numbers and email addresses of employees from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and other DHS component agencies.

Also included in the data were job titles and email groups, which, among other details, showed which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work.

In a statement, Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said the hacktivist and journalist known as “maia arson crimew” developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it. Best said the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability” and empower journalists, guide public records requests and boost congressional oversight. Crimew said her tool would provide “FOIA material for years to come!”

The Department of Peace did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but in a statement included with the data it said that DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction.”
The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors.

Best’s statement said the Department of Peace harvested the data from the Okta OKTA.O sign-on service used by DHS. Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim. Okta said in response to a Reuters query: “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.”

Reuters could not immediately verify the authenticity of the entire data trove but it was able to match personal information about six DHS employees named in the leak to credit bureau records and breach data carried by the dark web intelligence platform District 4 Labs. Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach.

In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees’ LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organization charts or previously undisclosed programs or operations. – Rappler.com
