articles.title: [Ask the Tax Whiz] BIR e-invoicing: Is your company ready for December 31?
articles.summary: This affects billing, customer records, accounting systems, and the controls that keep transactions accurate and traceable

blocks.text: The Philippine Tax Whiz explains what Revenue Memorandum Circular No. 98-2026 means for large taxpayers, multinational companies, and digital businesses—from permits and system requirements to branch coverage and billing errors.

Your company may already issue thousands of invoices through a global accounting system. But can it generate structured invoice data, deliver invoices electronically, and meet Philippine authorization requirements?
Under Revenue Memorandum Circular (RMC) No. 98-2026, covered taxpayers must comply with electronic invoicing requirements on or before December 31, 2026.

For chief financial officers, tax directors, and technology teams, this is a business readiness issue. It affects billing, customer records, accounting systems, and the controls that keep transactions accurate and traceable.
The circular identifies the following covered taxpayers, subject to its exemption for micro taxpayers:

items: Small, medium, and large taxpayers engaged in e-commerce or internet transactions;
Taxpayers under the jurisdiction of the Large Taxpayers Service (LTS);
Taxpayers classified as large under the Ease of Paying Taxes Act and Revenue Regulation (RR) No. 8-2024;
Taxpayers using a Computerized Accounting System (CAS), Computerized Books of Accounts with Accounting Records with electronic invoicing, or other invoicing software; and
Other taxpayers required by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue.

blocks.text: Companies should assess each applicable category. Being outside the Large Taxpayers Service (LTS) does not, by itself, establish exemption.
The definition of e-commerce also extends beyond online retail. It includes commercial transactions involving physical or digital goods and services conducted through electronic networks.

A Philippine subsidiary or registered branch should assess its own taxpayer classification, activities, and invoicing systems. Foreign ownership or the use of a regional billing center does not replace that assessment.
For multinational groups, the practical questions are: Which entity makes the sale? Which entity issues the invoice? Does its system meet Philippine requirements?

Nonresident digital service providers require a separate analysis. RR No. 3-2025 contains specific invoicing rules for nonresident VAT-registered providers, allowing electronic sales or commercial invoices that need not be registered with the BIR, provided prescribed information and language requirements are met. Companies should therefore avoid assuming that the domestic Permit to Issue (PTI) process automatically applies to every overseas platform selling to Philippine customers. (READ: [Ask the Tax Whiz] Guidelines on VAT for Nonresident Digital Service Providers)
An emailed PDF alone does not establish compliance.
Under RMC No. 98-2026, an electronic invoice must:

items: Be generated through duly registered, approved, or accredited accounting or invoicing software in a structured electronic format;
Be electronically generated and delivered through recognized electronic channels, such as email, online viewing, QR codes, applications, or web platforms; and
Contain data capable of electronic extraction, processing, and transmission to the BIR for sales reporting.

blocks.text: Invoices manually prepared using Word, Excel, Google Docs, Google Sheets, or similar productivity applications do not qualify.
A PDF may serve as the customer-facing copy of a compliant system-generated invoice. The underlying structured data and system capabilities remain essential.
Printed copies are also allowed under the circular and must be provided upon the buyer’s request. Printing an invoice does not cure a system that lacks the required electronic capabilities.
The circular separates electronic invoice issuance from electronic sales reporting.
Electronic invoicing concerns generating and issuing compliant invoices. Electronic sales reporting concerns transmitting sales data to the BIR.

Under RMC No. 98-2026, the electronic sales reporting obligation for the covered taxpayers is subject to the BIR’s issuance of implementing policies, guidelines, and procedures. The requirement to secure a Permit to Transmit applies upon notification or directive from the Commissioner.
Companies must prepare systems capable of transmission, but should not confuse that technical capability with an across-the-board reporting commencement date.
Taxpayers must secure a Permit to Issue (PTI) Electronic Invoice before generating or issuing electronic invoices.

The application must be filed with the Revenue District Office or Large Taxpayer Office where the taxpayer is registered, supported by the prescribed documents. The circular provides for evaluation and determination of compliance within 20 working days from receipt of complete documents.
An existing CAS Permit to Use or Acknowledgement Certificate does not, by itself, authorize electronic invoice issuance.
Taxpayers must also obtain Electronic Invoicing and Sales Reporting (EIS) Certification within six months from PTI issuance. Failure to obtain certification constitutes grounds for PTI revocation.

The certification validates the system’s ability to extract, process, and transmit sales data according to BIR standards. Technical specifications and guides are available through the EIS Certification Portal⁠.
The six-month certification period should not be treated as an extension of the December 31 invoicing deadline.
The circular allows an in-house solution, commercially acquired software, or services offered by an Electronic Invoicing Service Provider (ESP).

It also permits businesses to retain other structured formats for internal operations, provided the required sales data can be converted into and transmitted using the BIR-prescribed format. The existing EIS uses JavaScript Object Notation, or JSON, for sales data transmission.
For multinationals, this means assessing whether the current enterprise resource planning system can support Philippine requirements through configuration or integration.

As a practical readiness exercise, finance and IT teams should test customer and taxpayer identifiers, branch information, VAT treatment, discounts, withholding tax details, invoice references, and reconciliation with accounting records.

The circular reserves ESP policies and guidelines for a separate issuance. Businesses should verify a provider’s claimed authorization and distinguish vendor marketing from the taxpayer’s own permit and certification requirements.
Yes. Where the taxpayer is covered, compliance extends to its head office and all registered branches, even if the covered activity takes place only at a particular branch.

The circular provides for PTIs for the head office and individual branches bearing the same PTI number and identifying the relevant branch. However, each distinct invoicing system requires a separate PTI, identifying the offices or locations authorized to use it.
Changes to the approved platform or core system details—including migration or replacement—require a new or amended PTI, as applicable.
For corporations with multiple billing platforms, mapping systems to branches and business units should therefore be an early implementation step.
The obligation to issue invoices continues.

Where an interruption prevents electronic invoice issuance, the taxpayer must issue a BIR-authorized manual invoice. Once the system is restored, the manual invoices must be replaced with corresponding electronic invoices bearing their reference numbers.

For businesses, this calls for a documented contingency procedure: authorized manual invoices, clear staff responsibilities, and reconciliation after restoration to prevent missed or duplicate recording of sales.
No. Issued electronic invoices cannot be deleted, altered, or modified.
Corrections must use a separate document referencing the original invoice:

items: A decrease in the amount requires a duly authorized credit note or credit memo.
An increase requires a new electronic invoice.

blocks.text: If an invoice incorrectly states ₱50,000 instead of ₱5,000, a ₱45,000 credit note or memo corrects the overstatement while preserving the original record.

Companies should review whether their billing systems permit users to overwrite issued invoices. Approval controls and traceable adjustments are particularly important for high-volume billing, refunds, and subscription changes.
Moving to a lower classification does not automatically end the obligation. A covered taxpayer must continue complying unless the BIR expressly provides otherwise through a separate issuance.

For upward reclassification, the circular refers to a compliance period prescribed by the BIR that must not be less than six months from reclassification. This should not be described as a universal requirement to comply “within six months.”

Assign a joint finance, tax, and IT team to confirm coverage, map invoicing systems and branches, identify required changes, prepare PTI applications, and schedule certification testing. Include invoice corrections and outage recovery in testing—not just successful invoice generation.

Electronic invoicing can improve transaction visibility, reduce manual reconciliation, and strengthen tax administration. But implementation must also deliver clearer rules, secure systems, and less repetitive compliance.

For companies navigating complex systems or uncertain requirements, investing in advice from qualified tax experts early can help identify compliance gaps, prevent costly mistakes, and avoid unnecessary penalties and stress.

Electronic invoicing should make honest compliance easier—and deliberate tax evasion harder. Its success should translate into better data, simpler processes, and a more predictable environment for business and investment. – Rappler.com

articles.title: PH, Japan eye transfer of first Abukuma-class destroyer 'at the earliest possible date'
articles.summary: PH, Japan eye transfer of first Abukuma-class destroyer 'at the earliest possible date"

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 7:38am
The Philippines and Japan are working on transfer of the first Abukuma-class destroyer to the Philippine Navy at the earliest possible date.
In a joint statement after a defense meeting on Wednesday, the two countries said the Japanese warship will be transferred following its expected decommissioning in the coming years.

“Through this transfer, the two Ministers confirmed their intention to deepen comprehensive cooperation encompassing vessel operations, logistics support, human resource development, and information sharing, thereby taking defense cooperation, particularly in the field of maritime security, to a new level,” the joint statement read.

“They further confirmed that such cooperation would make a significant contribution to collaboration with allies and like-minded countries, thereby helping to ensuring peace and stability in the region,” it added.

Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. and Japanese Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro said defense authorities from both countries had agreed to pursue the transfer following discussions within a working group established in May.
Based on a report from Japanese media in July 2025, Tokyo is set to export six warships to the Philippines.
Teodoro and Koizumi also agreed to provide the necessary education and training for Philippine Navy personnel before the transfer and to cooperate closely on the vessel's maintenance and sustainment.

The planned transfer is expected to deepen Philippines-Japan defense cooperation, particularly in maritime security, through collaboration in vessel operations, logistics support, human resource development, and information sharing.
Teodoro and Koizumi said the cooperation would also contribute to collaboration with allies and like-minded countries, helping promote peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region.

The announcement came as the Philippines and Japan reaffirmed their opposition to unilateral attempts to change the status quo by force or coercion in the East China Sea and the South China Sea (SCS).

They also expressed serious concerns over China's increasingly frequent and extensive coercive activities in the waters and airspace surrounding Japan, as well as its dangerous and coercive actions against the Philippines in the South China Sea.
The two countries further committed to strengthening their bilateral defense ties under their Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and advancing efforts toward a Free and Open Indo-Pacific.
Meanwhile, the defense officials also agreed to discuss operational and maintenance arrangements for the transfer of a TC-90 aircraft to the Philippines by the end of Japan's fiscal year 2027.
They also agreed to accelerate discussions on defense equipment and technology cooperation, including efforts to strengthen the production base for defense equipment.

The Philippines and Japan have expanded military cooperation through joint exercises and agreements, including the Reciprocal Access Agreement and the Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement, which took effect in July 2026.
The Philippines is hosting the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) and the 13th ADMM-Plus on October 28 and 29 in Cebu.
ADMM is ASEAN's highest defense consultative and cooperative mechanism, according to the Department of National Defense (DND).
The ADMM-Plus expands defense cooperation to eight dialogue partners including Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia, and the United States. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: MTRCB reminds bus operators to screen only age-appropriate content for Undas
articles.summary: The Movie and Television Review and Classification Board (MTRCB) has started inspecting transport terminals across Metro Manila ahead of the expected surge of travelers heading to the provinces for…

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 7:16am

The Movie and Television Review and Classification Board (MTRCB) has started inspecting transport terminals across Metro Manila ahead of the expected surge of travelers heading to the provinces for All Saints’ Day, reminding bus operators to screen only age-appropriate content.
The spot inspections aim to ensure that films and other video content shown on buses comply with regulations, particularly as families and children are expected to travel during the Undas holiday.
MTRCB chairperson and CEO Lala Sotto urged transport terminals and operators to cooperate with the agency to ensure that content shown during trips is suitable for younger passengers.

“Hinihikayat namin ang kooperasyon ng mga transport terminals at operators nang masiguro natin na angkop mapanood ng mga batang pasahero ang mga ipapalabas sa mga bus habang sila ay pauwi ng probinsya para sa Undas,” Sotto said.

Under MTRCB Memorandum Circular No. 03-2024, or the “Rules Governing the Public Exhibition of Motion Picture and/or Trailers in Common Carriers and Other Public Places,” public utility vehicles may screen only films and trailers classified as General Audience (G) or Parental Guidance (PG).
The rules cover jeepneys, buses, vans, rail transport, taxis, passenger ships, ferry boats and commercial airplanes.
A G rating means a film is suitable for viewers of all ages, while a PG rating means younger viewers should be supervised by a parent or guardian.
During the inspections, MTRCB personnel reminded drivers and operators to ensure that all content shown to passengers complies with the prescribed classifications.
The inspections will continue through October 29, 2026.

The inspection and information campaign covers transport hubs in Muntinlupa, Las Piñas, Pasay, Parañaque, Quezon City, Taguig, Manila, Caloocan and Valenzuela, as well as Bocaue, Bulacan.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Non-profit group leaks data of more than 40,000 homeland security workers
articles.summary:
Information released by Distributed Denial of Secrets is the third such government data disclosure in the last month

The leak website Distributed Denial of Secrets said on Wednesday it has…

blocks.text: The leak website Distributed Denial of Secrets said on Wednesday it has released data on more than 40,000 Department ⁠of Homeland Security (DHS) employees, including details about officials working in sensitive fields such as surveillance and human intelligence.
DHS did not immediately return a message seeking comment.

The disclosure – which the ⁠non-profit data transparency group says draws ⁠on information obtained ​by an entity calling itself “Department of Peace” – is the third government data leak to have made headlines in the past month.

In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed ⁠the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees. Last week, the defense department was hit with ⁠a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel.

The DHS data includes ​names, phone numbers and email addresses of employees from Immigration ‌and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border ‌Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and other DHS component agencies.

Also included in the data were job ‌titles and email groups, which, among other details, showed which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work.

In a statement, Emma Best, a Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder, said the hacktivist known as “maia arson crimew” developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it. Best said the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability” and empower journalists, guide public records requests and boost congressional oversight.

The Department of Peace did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment, but in a statement included with the data, it said that DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can ​be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”.
The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors.

Best’s statement said Department of Peace harvested the data from the Okta sign-on service used by DHS. Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim. Okta said in response to a Reuters query: “Okta is ⁠secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.”

Reuters could not immediately ​verify the authenticity of the entire data ​trove but it was able to match ​personal information of about six DHS employees named in the leak to credit bureau records and breach data ​carried by the dark ‌web intelligence platform District 4 ​Labs. In other cases, ​Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach.

In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees’ LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organization charts or previously undisclosed programs or operations.

articles.title: Girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German wildlife park
articles.summary: The eight-year-old was in an enclosure with other children and a staff member when she was attacked.

blocks.text: An eight-year-old girl has been seriously injured in a wolf attack at a German wildlife park.
She was inside an enclosure at the Johannismühle park in Brandenburg, south of Berlin, with a staff member and two other children when the attack happened, police said.
They said in a statement that the "precise circumstances of the incident are the subject of an ongoing police investigation".
The girl was taken to hospital by helicopter after the incident on Wednesday. No one else was injured.
The park, in the town of Baruth/Mark, has been closed temporarily and is set to reopen on 2 November, according to its website, which did not give further details.
The park keeps grey and arctic wolves, along with other animals including the brown bear and lynx.
The girl was injured by at least one animal and suffered head injuries, according to German newspaper Bild.
It reported that the incident happened before the park opened at 10:00 local time (09:00 GMT) and that the girl could have been taking part in a special visit.
Johannismühle offers small group tours to allow visitors to spend time with some animals, with its site mentioning feeding wolves or petting a llama.
The incident comes after a number of other animal attacks at zoos and wildlife parks in Europe.
A keeper at a Dutch zoo died this week after being mauled by a leopard, and a man was killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park earlier this month.

articles.title: Australian SAS officers knew about unlawful ‘throwdowns’ on dead Afghans, report says
articles.summary:
Nothing done to stop planting weapons on dead Afghans, ADF inspector says, as ‘breakdown of command’ allowed ‘egregious behaviour’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Some Australian SAS officers knew that soldiers under their command were using “throwdowns” – planting weapons on dead Afghan civilians to portray them as combatants – but did nothing to stop the unlawful practice, a previously unpublished military report has said.

Posted online this week, the executive summary of a 2021 investigation into the “cultural context” of the special operations command by the inspector general of the Australian Defence Force (IGADF) is scathing about the “breakdown of command” and the erosion of military discipline during special forces operations in Afghanistan, which “resulted in episodes of potential and actual egregious behaviour”.

A previously published IGADF report, the Brereton Inquiry, made public in 2020, found credible information that Australian special forces personnel murdered 39 Afghan civilians and prisoners. But the Brereton report largely exonerated officers, saying the “criminal behaviour” it uncovered “was conceived, committed, continued, and concealed at patrol commander level”. Patrol commanders in the Australian SAS are not commissioned officers, they are typically corporals or sergeants.

However, the newly released report, commissioned after the Brereton findings by former defence force chief – and SAS officer – Angus Campbell in 2021, found some SAS officers knew about alleged “unlawful behaviour” and did not act to stop them.

“Officers with actual knowledge of misconduct in-theatre, including notably the use of throwdowns to effect in fraudulent reporting, or rumours of misconduct, did not take effective action to investigate and address these issues.”
The unlawful behaviour identified by the IGADF revealed “a breakdown of command” and ineffective leadership.

“The proper functioning of the ADF as a hierarchical system relies upon the enforcement of rules at all levels. A failure to do so has a corrosive effect on behaviours, morale and ultimately, military discipline, which in this case resulted in episodes of potential and actual egregious behaviour.”

SAS officers allowed the regiment to develop an “uncontrolled ‘warrior’ ethos” and the long, grinding, nature of the Afghan conflict, to which a small cohort of SAS soldiers were repeatedly sent on dangerous, corrosive deployments, contributed to moral injury and impaired decision-making.
“The group dynamic within a special forces deployment influences the shift in moral compass of some individuals,” the report said.
“The incremental shift in moral compass in response to violence, killing, morally questionable decisions and unconventional features, can create moral injury.”

The report found that the excessively secretive and insular nature of the SAS also contributed to worsening standards as did an “inversion” of the chain of command, where senior non-commissioned officers were able to dominate officers who were, ostensibly, their superiors.
“This resulted in junior officers being effectively subservient to non-commissioned officers, and occupying a position which can best be described as ‘learned helplessness’.”

The report cited the fact SAS soldiers were consistently allowed to drink alcohol while on deployment in Afghanistan – in defiance of orders imposed on others – “sent the strong signal to those involved that the rules did not apply to them”.
The use of “throwdowns” was a known breach that officers failed to stop.

“The unwillingness to challenge non-commissioned officers was particularly apparent from the breakdown of military discipline through a lack of proper supervision. The failure to address the widely known use of throwdowns is an example of this.
“This was also a manifestation of a broader breakdown of military discipline within the SAS regiment. The tolerance of officers of overt non-compliance sent a powerful signal.”

Similarly, soldiers wrote false reports of their actions on the battlefield, focused on rules of engagement and laced with circumlocution, which “assisted perpetrators of misconduct to conceal their actions”.

“A particular manifestation was the use of variations of a standard phrase ‘manoeuvring to a position of tactical advantage’, to describe the actions of civilian ‘squirters’ as direct participants in hostilities, which justified engagement … under the rules of engagement. The expression was used with such regularity that it lost meaning.”

The report’s executive summary says there was “a significant failure of good leadership and effective command” across the SAS commanders, and that the reporting systems designed to prevent misconduct had become “depleted and largely unreliable”, giving officers “a false level of assurance”.
“The culture of the Special Operations Task Group … was not the cause of misconduct but created an environment which enabled misconduct by a few to occur.”
Defence had previously refused to release the report despite it being the subject of freedom of information requests and an attempt to force its disclosure in the Senate.

articles.title: New book makes fiery claims about Jared Kushner’s finances in Trump’s first term
articles.summary:
Kushner threatens to sue, denying allegations that two slush funds were set up to influence his Middle East role

A new book containing incendiary claims about

blocks.text: A new book containing incendiary claims about Jared Kushner’s financial dealings during Donald Trump’s first term has ignited a political and media firestorm.

The book by author Matthew Cole is called Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East and was released in the US this week. An excerpt was published by Vanity Fair last Thursday, and immediately drew a furious response from Kushner, who called its claims “completely insane”. The book contains numerous allegations about Kushner, whose father-in-law is Trump and who has served as one of his top diplomatic envoys in the Middle East – the most explosive of which are claims linking him to huge bank accounts allegedly funded by Gulf states.

Kusher denounced the book on his site last week, and writing on X: “We denied every one of these claims on the record, yet the author failed to provide a single shred of evidence to substantiate any of them.” He has demanded that Vanity Fair retract the excerpt and has threatened legal action against the book’s publisher, Simon & Schuster.

He added: “During the period in question, I was one of the most scrutinized people in the world, subjected to intense media coverage, multiple congressional investigations, and a special counsel investigation. I voluntarily cooperated with these investigations, providing over 30 hours of testimony. None of these allegations ever surfaced, because none of these events ever happened.”
The Guardian contacted Kushner’s legal counsel from Clare Locke as well as Chad Mizelle for comment and received no response.

Cole’s sources are predominantly anonymous and he does not print images of emails or other documentation to support his reporting. Extensive footnotes indicate sources of information, including confidential interviews.

In the book, the top intelligence official in the United Arab Emirates, Ali Al Shamsi, is reported to have called Kushner “the most expensive employee we’ve ever had”. The book details alleged payments into two “slush fund” bank accounts allegedly set up for Kushner by Emirati prince Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) and Saudi Arabian prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) during Trump’s first term. The Guardian contacted the Saudi Arabian and Emirati embassies for comment and did not receive a response.
In the book, Cole claims the accounts were partially managed by Kushner on an iPhone hacked by Russian and Dutch intelligence.

But despite the Emirati spymaster’s opinion of Kushner, Cole alleges that the New Jersey real estate scion was not entirely trusted. Cole describes a dangerous world in which blackmail is as common a tool of statecraft as torture and murder, as in the cases of the Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, killed on the orders of MBS in Turkey in 2018, and the Emirati journalist and poet Habib Al Sayegh, whose killing by agents of MBZ in 2019 is described by Cole.

Kushner continues to steer US foreign policy despite having no official role, with questions about his business interests accompanying him as he travels the world with New York real estate magnate Steve Witkoff, this week seeking peace in Ukraine, if on terms favorable to Russia.

In response, an attorney “who has represented President Trump in multiple defamation lawsuits”, Alejandro Brito, told Cole that, “during his time working for President Trump, Kushner ‘always represented and sought the interests of the United States and the President of the United States and did not make any agreements or arrangements with leaders or officials in foreign countries that were not agreed by the President of the United States and in the best interests of the United States.’” He further said that “[a]ny allegation that Kushner knew of, had access to, had authorization for or engaged in or directed any conduct related to any government-funded or government-linked bank account is totally false and defamatory”.
Brito told Cole that “‘there are no accounts and never were.’” Cole writes that the Dutch government refused to comment in response to his questions about the alleged hacking of Kushner’s phone.

According to Cole, MBZ and MBS wanted Kushner to help achieve their “vision of a new Middle East, one in which Israel would become an integral part of the region, recognized diplomatically by Gulf Arabs today and eventually by the rest of the Arab world; the Palestinians would end their conflict with Israel and accept a peace built on prosperity; Islamic extremism would be defeated; and Iran’s expansionism and militancy would retreat, either by persuasion or force.”

Nearly 10 years later, the US and Israel are planning new strikes in their eight-month war with Iran; Saudi Arabia is at war with Houthi rebels in Yemen, and Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023.

Kushner entered Trump’s first administration with his wife, Ivanka Trump, as close presidential advisers. MBZ and MBS, Cole claims, saw a chance to secure the best access money could buy. Cole alleges that in early 2017 the two princes “proposed to give Kushner a fund, a bank account, which the two leaders, working with Jared, would use to identify and pay for projects and foreign policy goals to advance for President Trump’s benefit”.

According to Cole, an idea to fund Trump’s proposed wall on the US border with Mexico apparently did not work out but the author claims that “MBZ and MBS initially, and then MBZ alone, put at least $2bn into at least two banks for Kushner.” Classifying the accounts as “Alpha” and “Beta”, Cole claims the Alpha account was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, the largest in UAE, and contained “roughly $750m” to be “used as a foreign policy fund” overseen by Kushner and MBZ and meant to help end the Israel-Palestine conflict.

Cole quotes a source who says he knew of the UAE’s alleged deal with Kushner as saying: “‘Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy.’” Cole writes: “This person held discussions with both senior UAE and Israeli officials about the secret financial arrangement between Kushner, the UAE, and, at least initially, Saudi Arabia. ‘Jared promised MBZ that he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalization with Israel so that business could take off,’” the source alleged.

The same source claimed that “a slush fund – a shared pool of money for off-the-books diplomatic objectives – was a common form of Gulf Arab government corruption … ‘The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent.’”

Citing “a person briefed on the Beta account”, Cole claims it contained “roughly $1bn” and at the suggestion of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was moved by MBZ to the Israeli Central Bank via Azerbaijan, a favored conduit for laundering money.

“It is … unclear how Kushner used the money the UAE deposited into the Beta account for him,” Cole alleges, “but according to the person with knowledge of the money, its allocation was for Kushner’s personal benefit.”

Kushner’s attorney, Brito, told Cole his client “had no financial relationships with any foreign countries or leaders”, adding that his “complete financial disclosures are publicly available in his OGE [office of government ethics] form 278e filings during this period.”

Cole alleges that the “Alpha” account established for Kushner in Trump’s first term was drained by failed schemes and Kushner’s access was cut off. “It is unclear if the Israeli government allowed Kushner access to the Beta bank account” after the end of Trump’s first term, Cole writes.

Cole also examines the widely reported story about how Kushner ultimately secured Qatari investment in 666 Fifth Avenue, a marquee Manhattan property, thereby profiting from interests on both sides of a bitterly divided Middle East, given Saudi Arabia and UAE’s rivalry with Qatar. (Kushner has denied engaging in any conflicts of interest.)

In Trump’s second term, Kushner’s diplomatic work has been dogged by questions about another massive financial asset: a $2bn investment by the Saudi sovereign wealth fund in Kushner’s Affinity Partners private equity firm, made after Trump left power in 2021. Cole quotes an unnamed Arab official and Affinity investor who claimed: “We don’t pay Jared because he’s a savvy investor. We pay him to keep him happy. That keeps his father-in-law happy.”

Cole writes: “Deep relationships with MBZ, MBS, Emir Al Thani [of Qatar], and Bibi Netanyahu were useful as [Kushner] shuttled between capitals, trying to find a way to end the daily slaughter in Gaza. But as it had been when he was a government employee, there was little record of what his investors were negotiating with him.”

In his epilogue, Cole writes that Kushner “declined multiple requests for an on-the-record interview for the book”, adding that he “first contacted him with a list of questions in May 2026 and followed up via email twice more, asking additional questions.”

Through his lawyers, Kushner denounced all of Cole’s reporting. Also on X, Chad Mizelle, a Trump administration lawyer who identified himself as “Jared’s attorney”, said: “The central allegation in this book is categorically false. These are not questions of interpretation or competing recollections: there are no bank accounts. They don’t exist. These are egregious and defamatory claims without a shred of evidence to substantiate them.”

articles.title: Dolores Huerta, U.S. labour leader and civil rights icon, dead at 96
articles.summary: Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in fruit and vegetable fields in the United States and coined the enduring "Sí, se puede!" rallying cry, has…

image.caption: United Farm Workers leader Dolores Huerta pictured in November 1988. Huerta kept busy well into her 90s, marching in protests and encouraging activists to keep speaking out about race, poverty, and 2SLGBTQ+ and women's rights. (Court Mast/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in fruit and vegetable fields in the United States and coined the enduring "Sí, se puede!" rallying cry, has died. She was 96.
Huerta died of cancer Wednesday at her home in Bakersfield, Calif., surrounded by family, said family spokesperson Erik Olvera.
Huerta kept busy well into her 90s, marching in protests and encouraging activists to keep speaking out about race, poverty, and 2SLGBTQ+ and women's rights.
"It seems like history continues to repeat itself," she told the Associated Press in August. "You see what's happening right now in our country, and we know that people have to stand up."

Huerta's resolve cemented her place as one of the most influential labour leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists in U.S. history. Her Spanish slogan "Sí, se puede" — "Yes, it can be done" — was grounded in the belief that people who take action can affect change.

Her accolades over the decades included the U.S. Presidential Medal of Freedom. When then-president Barack Obama presented her with the nation's highest civilian honour in 2012, he praised Huerta as a tenacious leader and said she was gracious when he stole her slogan for his 2008 presidential campaign.
"I'm pleased that she let me off easy … 'cause Dolores does not play," Obama joked.

"Her life's work was to empower her community to face and overcome injustices, and she has left farm workers and the entire Latino community stronger and more organized than she found it," United Farm Workers president Teresa Romero said in a statement Wednesday.
Barack Obama awards Dolores Huerta the Presidential Medal of Freedom on May 29, 2012. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)
60-year secret that shook Latino culture

Huerta revealed earlier this year that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by the farmworker movement's co-founder, César Chavez, leading to the birth of two children — a secret she had kept for 60 years, long after he died.
Chavez's reputation immediately soured, his name removed from streets and buildings and the holiday that had been a point of Hispanic pride.

items: U.S. civil rights leader Dolores Huerta says Cesar Chavez sexually assaulted her in the 1960s

blocks.text: Huerta said she had kept silent for so long because she feared coming forward would compromise her life's work and unravel all the progress made for workers. From the early 1970s on, Huerta's life partner had been Richard Chavez, César's brother, and together they had four children. She also had seven children from two earlier marriages.

Earlier this year, when asked during an interview with news organization Latino USA about keeping the secret, Huerta said: "It was my personal pain, it was my personal problem and, you know, I think it was worth it because it was my cross to bear. I'll say it that way."

Huerta stands beside a 1998 portrait of herself, taken by photographer Angela Torres, as she tours a Los Angeles exhibition focused on her life's work in April 2014. (Damian Dovarganes/The Associated Press)
'Passion for justice and fairness'

Huerta's advocacy changed many lives beyond the farm fields, said former U.S. president Bill Clinton and former secretary of state Hillary Rodham Clinton, who called her "a stalwart champion of working Americans."

"Dolores wore many hats: voting rights advocate, human rights champion, die-hard Democrat, self-described ‘born-again feminist,' and co-founder of the United Farm Workers of America," the Clintons said in a statement. "To see her in action was to witness a living legend who never stopped pushing for progress."
California Gov. Gavin Newsom said his state would not be where it is without her "passion for justice and fairness."
"Dolores's fight for gender equity, workers' rights, and civil rights paved the way for generations to come — teaching people what was possible with determination and heart," Newsom said.
Huerta, left, with Hillary Clinton, centre, and senator Dianne Feinstein in February 2008. (Paul Sakuma/The Associated Press)

Huerta was born Dolores Clara Fernandez in 1930 in Dawson, N.M. Her father was a miner and union activist who won a seat in the state legislature. Her parents divorced when she was three, and her mother took her and her brothers to California.

Immersed in a melting pot of Mexican, Filipino, African American, Japanese and Chinese working families, Huerta learned from her mother — who owned a restaurant and hotel — about independence, compassion and activism.

Huerta was a young, energetic elementary school teacher in the agricultural San Joaquin Valley when she decided to answer another calling after growing frustrated by her students' poor living conditions.

"I couldn't stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes," she said in a 2017 PBS documentary on her life. "I thought I could do more by organizing farm workers than by trying to teach their hungry children."

items: Helen Chavez, widow of labour leader Cesar Chavez, dead at 88

blocks.text: Huerta's early work with a civil rights group in Stockton resulted in her meeting Chavez. The two wanted to focus more on the plight of farm workers, so in 1962 they started the National Farm Workers Association, which became United Farm Workers of America a few years later. She was a key leader and negotiator for the union for years.

She was among those who joined Filipino grape pickers on the picket line in what became the five-year Delano Grape Strike. With Chavez, she negotiated collective bargaining agreements and contracts with big growers, winning the first health and benefit plans for farm workers.
Chavez, who died in 1993, once described her as fearless, committed to the cause and tough when it came to negotiations.
Campaigning for presidents and women's rights

She met Sen. Robert Kennedy in 1968 and volunteered with his presidential campaign, registering Mexican Americans in California to vote. Huerta was on stage with Kennedy in Los Angeles after he won the California primary and he publicly thanked her, moments before he was fatally shot.
The assassination devastated Huerta, but she kept organizing. Huerta was jailed 22 times for union demonstrating.
In 1988, she was seriously injured while protesting Republican presidential candidate George H.W. Bush's opposition to the UFW grape boycott during his visit to San Francisco.

Caught in a crowd, she was struck by a police officer's baton, suffered three broken ribs and a pulverized spleen and required blood transfusions. She reached a settlement with the city to resolve her claims.
After a long recovery, Huerta shifted focus, campaigning for women's rights and encouraging Latino women to run for office.
She also campaigned for Democratic presidents Clinton, Obama and Joe Biden.
'We want to give our children an inheritance of justice'
Emilio Huerta, one of Dolores's 13 children, said his mother's courage drove her life's work.
"To dedicate your life to building a dream of a union for farm workers, to take on agriculture, which to this day is still a powerhouse … That took a lot of guts," he said.

Huerta secured financial aid for the unemployed and disability insurance for California farm workers. She spoke out against toxic pesticides, pushed for amnesty for immigrants in the country illegally and campaigned against federal guest worker programs.

By directing nationwide boycotts of grapes and lettuce in the early 1970s, she helped to create the economic pressure and political climate necessary for California to pass the first state law recognizing farm workers' right to collective bargaining.

Huerta's leadership in the labour movement made her name synonymous with civil rights in the U.S. and beyond. In the 2025 documentary Seeds of Change: The Life and Legacy of Dolores Huerta, she credited the 1970s women's movement for providing her with the validation to take the stage with other labor leaders.
"I hope that my legacy will be one of an organizer that organized to fight injustice," she said in the film.

"We want to give our children an inheritance of justice … not jewels or property or money because they'll just fight over it. So the main thing to do is to give them this love for justice — and that is the greatest gift I think that any of us can have."

articles.title: High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
articles.summary: The crash, between a moving train and another that was stopped further up the track, was caused by an "inexplicable" error, the transport minister said.

blocks.text: A high-speed train crash has killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more in central Spain.

It occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into another train - which was stationary on the tracks - on Wednesday morning. The force saw several carriages fall down an embankment.
The transport minister said a computer failure followed by human error caused the collision, which is one of the worst in Europe's modern history, and Spain's deadliest train disaster in 13 years.
Survivors described harrowing scenes of passengers being thrown into the air, trapped in the wreckage and smashing windows to get out.
The collision happened just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) around 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid.
The stationary train, run by private rail operator Iryo, had 147 passengers on board, and had stopped on the tracks because of a computer failure, Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said.

He explained that when there is a system failure, a 24-hour control centre in Madrid takes over, but it had made an "inexplicable" decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by another train, run by Spain's state-owned railway company, Renfe, which was carrying 397 passengers.
The force of the crash was "brutal", said 62-year-old passenger Salvador Arriza who was sitting in the Renfe-operated train.
Passengers started breaking the windows to get out, he told Reuters, adding that "some people couldn't move because they were trapped amongst the seats."
One of the carriages caught fire, and passengers described devastating scenes of trapped people crying and bleeding, with some buried under debris.
Pictures show that a long piece of railway track had speared through one of the carriages.
Spanish journalist Antonio Jiménez Barca, who works for El Pais newspaper, was walking to the Renfe train's cafeteria when the crash happened.
"I felt like I was being pushed from behind, like I was being thrown to the ground," he described.
"I hit my head horribly... I was covered in blood. There were people on top of me. One person had an injured arm, and another had a head injury."
Another passenger, 46-year-old Sebastián Herrero, told El Mundo newspaper that he saw "many people with broken noses, broken arms."
"It was a terrible, terrible impact," he said, adding that he was "in the air for about four or five seconds," which felt like a lifetime.
Many of the passengers said they were in shock, and one sobbed during an interview with a local television station as he described a woman dying in his arms.
"She was very cold and she was all alone," he said, to which the show's presenter also started to cry.
Dozens of ambulances rushed to the scene, and a helicopter evacuated those with the most serious injuries.
Spain's Civil Guard said it would need DNA samples from relatives to identify some victims.
"The whole of Spain is grieving", Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said during a visit to the crash site. "Lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart, the pain is immense."
Spain was already reeling from a high-speed rail disaster near Córdoba in January that killed 46 people. It happened on the same rail line, but much further south.
Wednesday's crash is the worst the country has seen since 2013, when when 80 people died on the outskirts of Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain.
"Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure," said Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the the main opposition People's Party.
Spanish trade union CSIF has demanded the transport minister resign, accusing him of "scapegoating" a traffic manager, by blaming human error in the control room, instead of "taking responsibility".
Sánchez and other Spanish politicians cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.
The prime minister said it was "unacceptable" for Spain to have two serious train crashes in one year, and vowed to "get to the bottom of this" and determine if there was any negligence.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."

articles.title: Bloodied, dazed and angry - how passengers' rail journey turned to disaster in Spain
articles.summary: Survivors of the train crash in Spain have spoken of their shock, panic and anger at the accident in Toledo province on Wednesday.

blocks.text: Broken arms, broken noses, rail through the roof
Some of the passengers were asleep, some had already started their working day on laptops - and others scrolled through their apps on their phones.
The journey was interrupted with an announcement that there was congestion on the tracks. This lasted a few minutes - for some, a bit longer for others.
Tangui Binier, 22, was in the Iryo train, the front carriage, number eight. His father was in number seven.
Their train was one of six to have been ordered to stop at 08:30. A few minutes later, "the train started speeding", Binier told the BBC, "then it came to a sudden halt".
Baffled, he looked out of the window and saw "wires on the left side come down, and then there being just a lot of smoke behind us."
Spanish journalist Roberto Gómez was dozing on the high-speed Renfe train which had stopped more than 25km (16 miles) away from Binier's.
It was a brief stop. A few minutes later, the train began to move again, he explained, and then the crash happened.
He did not know that at 08:36 his train had been ordered to proceed with the journey and some 17 minutes later the "truly unbelievable" happened, Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said.
"The impact was terrible," Gómez told Onda Cero radio. "You can imagine, the carriage is completely destroyed. All the suitcases are all over the wrecked carriage."
Gómez suffered only minor injuries but described another passenger falling on top of him and sustaining a deep gash on his head.
"We were able to help people who had suffered severe blows to their chest and ribs," he said.
Rafael Barcelo was in one of the worst-affected carriages. A bruise on his forehead makes him one of the lucky survivors. He was having a coffee at the time of the crash and "felt a huge impact".
"We were all thrown into the air," he told Reuters news agency at the site of the crash.
"I am reasonably OK, my friend is quite worse."
"I was travelling in coach seven, which is the one with more victims and the one most destroyed. I at least counted eight victims in that coach," he said, visibly shocked.
Once the initial impact was over, passengers in Binier's carriage debated whether it was safe to leave because of the electrical wires strewn outside the train.
Some were worried about the risk of another train colliding and decided to exit.
"We did not know what had happened until we took a step outside, and there there was evidence of what had happened.
"We saw the other train behind ours and we saw our train completely flipped over and the back side full of debris," he told the BBC.
"When I got out of the train I was in complete shock, complete awe. There were people in danger, it was very hard to see, there was dead bodies, there was missing limbs. "
"I don't know if that is something I will ever recover from."
But the adrenaline kicked in, he said, and those like him who had not suffered any injuries went to help.
Among them was his dad, who he explained was "able to carry a girl to safety, with a broken hip".
It was not long before local people arrived, followed by the police and ambulance services of the Guardia Civil.

"I'm really one of the most fortunate people and the luckiest person. I feel like just I'm so fortunate and I see other people who are not so fortunate, and I see them very close up. Sometimes you just ask yourself 'Why me?'," he said.

articles.title: Death of US actress Hayden Panettiere ruled accidental, ending local police probe
articles.summary: The Heroes and Nashville star died in August from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs.

blocks.text: The death of US actress Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, ending a local probe in her death, police in South Carolina have said.
The Heroes and Nashville star died in August from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, at the age of 36.
Citing the medical examiner's report last month that found Panettiere died from a drug overdose, the Greenville Police Department said it had "concluded its investigation" into her death.
The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) reportedly joined a local police probe. It is unclear if that investigation has also concluded. The BBC has contacted the DEA for comment.
"Based on the Medical Examiner's determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere's death has been ruled accidental," police said in a statement.
Authorities, including the DEA, were reportedly investigating the circumstances of Panettiere's death, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

articles.title: EU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talks
articles.summary:
Watered-down version of statement to be issued at end of Montreal summit instead offers ‘ever closer association’

The EU has backed away from its offer to Canada to start talks on becoming…
articles.byline: Lisa O’Carroll in Brussels and Leyland Cecco in Toronto

blocks.text: The EU has backed away from its offer to Canada to start talks on becoming an “associate member” after disagreements between members states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal.

A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”.

The issue was triggered after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, surprised nearly everyone by announcing in last month’s state of the union address that the EU would consider “associate membership” for Canada.
The declaration had been hailed as a landmark in EU history, offering a non-EU country such close ties to the bloc, which has not allowed any state membership since Croatia joined in 2013.
It was also seen as a sign that the call by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, at the Davos summit in January for “middle powers” to work together was paying off.

But instead of announcing a work programme on developing “associate membership”, the draft communique, seen by the Guardian, states the two sides would “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy”.
Associate membership had been mooted, and rejected, previously for countries such as Ukraine.

Von der Leyen’s declaration caught EU capitals by surprise and led to pushback politically and legally. Given “associate status” has no definition, diplomats wondered about such issues as whether Canada could join the European Council, legislative bodies or decision-making processes without a vote.

At a meeting on Monday, ambassadors in the EU raised concerns about the dramatic offer, but vowed to make efforts to seek a diplomatic path to rescinding the offer of “associate” membership without embarrassing Von der Leyen. It is understood that Italy suggested “associate membership as proposed by the commission”, with the definition to be thrashed out later by member states.
Germany walked back further, suggesting the wording “an ever closer association of Canada” to the EU.

“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [Von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem. Many member states, including Germany, were not happy. This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying,” said one diplomat.

Germany had argued that “associate membership” should be reserved as an interim step for prospective candidate countries, such as Ukraine or Montenegro, noting that the status has no formal grounding in current EU treaties.

Donald Trump, the US president, previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable”, and said if he ​interpreted the move as a “hostile act” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.

A bitter trade war with the US, a longtime ally, has seen Carney seek out new trading partnerships around the world. Ahead of the summit in Montreal, one of Canada’s largest banks released a report suggesting there was “meaningful” upside for Canada if it were to deepen economic ties with Europe. Tens of billions of dollars in additional trade would be possible if barriers were removed in areas of overlapping interest such as defence, energy, critical minerals and digital markets, TD Economics said.
Carney has spoken specifically about the need to lessen reliance on Elon Musk‘s Starlink satellite network, following a decision to throttle its usage over Ukraine.

Earlier this week, Carney posted on social media that Canada would join the popular music competition Eurovision. But despite fears raised by political rivals, Carney has said Canada has no interest in formally joining the EU. Changing Canadian laws to bring it in line with European nations would probably prove unpopular, despite public support for stronger ties.
Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week was the launch of further formal negotiations that will take place another year.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about ⁠specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will ​make to the lives ​of Canadians.”
A previous draft statement ​had included at least two references to Canada as an “associate member”, ​including an acknowledgment that ‌defining the ​term would take ​another year.

articles.title: Three face murder charges in death of 12-year-old boy found in rural Alberta
articles.summary: Insp. Wayne Stevenson of the RCMP’s serious crime branch said at a news conference Wednesday in Edmonton that Fiasal "was associated with people involved in criminality" and knew the three accused.…

image.caption: The death of Fiasal Hussein, 12, was declared a homicide by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner. (RCMP)

blocks.text: Edmonton

Insp. Wayne Stevenson of the RCMP’s serious crime branch said at a news conference Wednesday in Edmonton that Fiasal "was associated with people involved in criminality" and knew the three accused. Stevenson alleged that Fiasal was lured from his home before being killed.
Body of Fiasal Hussein was found near Calling Lake, Alta. in August
Three people from Edmonton have been charged in the death of a 12-year-old boy whose remains were found in rural Alberta in August.

The boy has been identified as Fiasal Hussein by police. Cole Morin, 34, and Curtis Brown, 36, have been charged with first-degree murder and kidnapping. Rachel Stuart, 36, has been charged with second-degree murder.

"He did not deserve that,” said Stevenson. “Whatever challenges or choices may have led to his untimely death, he was still a child with a future ahead of him. This was a cruel and heartbreaking act.”

Stevenson said the investigation began with a 911 call to Athabasca RCMP shortly before 3:30 a.m. on Aug .6. The unknown caller, who police now believe was Fiasal, said he had been kidnapped and was injured.

items: RCMP investigating homicide of 12-year-old Edmonton boy after remains found in northern Alberta

blocks.text: The call came from the area around Calling Lake, Alta., which is about 200 kilometres north of Edmonton. Spotty reception made it difficult for dispatchers to assess the situation, said Stevenson.

Officers arriving at the scene found a vehicle that had been reported stolen from Edmonton. Stevenson said officers found evidence of an attack, but did not comment on its nature. Hussein’s remains were found at around 9 a.m. during a search of the area. The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner declared the death to be a homicide.
Brown, Morin and Stuart were arrested at residences throughout Edmonton on Oct. 24. All three remain in custody and are scheduled to appear in the Athabasca Court of Justice on Nov. 9.

Police did not elaborate on the relationship between Fiasal and the three accused. They also didn’t provide details on how the boy left his house or how he was killed. Sgt. James McConnell with the RCMP’s major crimes unit said those details are part of the investigation and will be told in court.
“The exact specifics and motive of this homicide are still part of the ongoing investigation,“ said McConnell.
"Parents aren’t supposed to bury their children and that’s what we have in this case.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Vincent McDermott covers Fort McMurray and the Wood Buffalo region for CBC News. He was previously the editor of Fort McMurray Today, where he was part of a team that won a National Newspaper Award for coverage of the 2016 Horse River Wildfire. He is also a former contributor to the official magazine of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada. He can be reached at vincent.mcdermott@cbc.ca

articles.title: Game 6 of the WNBA Finals starts at 12:30 p.m. ET tomorrow. How did this happen?
articles.summary: CBC Sports' daily newsletter breaks down the scheduling fiasco that caused Game 6 of the WNBA Finals to be moved to a weekday afternoon, and what it means for a league that can't seem to avoid…

image.caption: Game 6 of the WNBA Finals between Angel Reese's Atlanta Dream and the Golden State Valkyries will tip off at 12:30 p.m. ET due to an arena scheduling conflict. (Ezra Shaw/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Basketball·THE BUZZER

CBC Sports' daily newsletter breaks down the scheduling fiasco that caused Game 6 of the WNBA Finals to be moved to a weekday afternoon, and what it means for a league that can't seem to avoid controversy.
Finals scheduling fiasco is the league's latest controversy
The hottest topic in sports discourse this week is the WNBA Finals.

Not the actual games, though. Not whether two-way star Angel Reese can lead the Atlanta Dream to their first-ever championship. Not whether the Golden State Valkyries can win the title in just their second year of existence. Not even whether this is maybe not the most exciting matchup as these teams are averaging only 69 points per game apiece in the series after Caitlin Clark's Indiana Fever averaged 96 in the regular season.

Instead, everyone is firing off takes about the unusual start time of tomorrow's Game 6 and whether the league should have moved it to a different time and/or place. That's right, to paraphrase Allen Iverson: We talkin' about… logistics?

To be fair, that start time is extremely bizarre: 12:30 p.m. ET, which puts it at 9:30 a.m. ET in the Bay Area as Golden State looks to finish off the series with a win. While this may conjure nostalgic black-and-white images of stickball-playing Brooklyn kids ditching school to listen to the 1955 World Series on the transistor radio, a weekday afternoon championship game is obviously quite suboptimal in today's broadcast-focused age.
So, why is this happening?

It starts with the decision to move the Dream's home Finals games from their usual 3,500-seat arena to the 17,000-seat home of the NBA's Atlanta Hawks. It paid off as both of the Atlanta-hosted games so far were sell-outs — including last Saturday's Game 4, which was moved up 2½ hours to 1 p.m. ET because the Hawks had their home opener that night.

The earlier start time on Saturday wasn't a big deal because sports fans are accustomed to weekend matinees. But weekdays are a different story, and the WNBA found itself in quite the pickle when Golden State won that Game 4 to even the best-of-seven Finals at two games apiece and guarantee a Game 6 in Atlanta on Thursday.

The Hawks, who are the primary tenant at State Farm Arena, are scheduled to host the Cleveland Cavaliers there on Thursday night, and getting the NBA to bump that game to another day or change it to a matinee was a non-starter. Pushing Game 6 to Friday night was nixed because the cable USA Network, which is sharing the U.S. broadcast rights for the Finals with NBC this year, had already committed to showing horse racing's Breeders' Cup and WWE wrestling that evening. Plus, a potential Game 7 is slated for the next day on the other side of the country in San Francisco.
Pair of options

So, that left the WNBA with a pair of options, both unappealing in their own way: keep Game 6 in primetime and go back to the tiny arena, or start it early enough to clear out in time for the Hawks but risk alienating the national TV audience.

They went with the bigger gate. And cue the outrage from fans, pundits and even the owners of the Dream, who published a rather emotional open letter last night claiming they flagged these potential scheduling issues two months ago and "reiterated" them during the playoffs but their concerns "did not receive the attention nor the urgency that they deserved."

The players, though, are mostly taking it in stride. "Call in sick," Golden State guard Veronica Burton urged her team's fans, while forward Kiah Stokes joked: "Don't y'all know know to fake a cough?" Atlanta Coach Karl Smesko, tongue in cheek, called for a national holiday.
But this is no laughing matter for the WNBA, which is once again under fire for something that is happening off the court.

Between the lines, the league has never been better, with Clark and other stars like Reese, fifth-time MVP A'ja Wilson, high-scoring guard Paige Bueckers and super rookie Olivia Miles pushing the quality of play to new heights and driving unprecedented attendance, TV ratings and general interest in the WNBA. But the league has also been dogged by culture-war proxy battles like whether it should promote Clark as the face of the majority-black league and what Fever standout Sophie Cunningham thinks about the hot-button issue of trans people in women's sports.

You could argue that the WNBA didn't start these fires, and that it's fallen victim to opportunistic (and extremely online) culture warriors who don't actually care about women's basketball and are just using it to further their own ends. That's broadly correct. But, as I wrote back in the summer when the Cunningham controversy was dominating the discourse, the WNBA has shown little ability (or even interest) in calming things down and putting the focus back on hoops.
Then again, they say we're in an attention economy. And the WNBA has shown once again that it is very good at attracting attention.

articles.title: Israel's election deadlock is a sign of the country's deep divisions
articles.summary: The election was a celebration of democracy in some ways - but it has left Israel with no clear path to a new government, writes James Landale.

blocks.text: "Democracy is the worst form of government except for all those other forms that have been tried." So said Winston Churchill in the House of Commons in 1947.
His aphorism came to mind as Israel's election results filtered through on Tuesday night - exit polls blending with ballots that were cast to dash or fulfil people's hopes and fears.
This election has, in some ways, been a celebration of democracy. Voters turning out in record numbers, Jews and Arabs alike. Many spent thousands to fly in from abroad to cast their ballot.
At polling stations across the country, we saw the passion of campaigners, as they used every minute to try to change that last mind and win that last vote.
President Isaac Herzog said the election was a "badge of honour" for Israeli society. "It is remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he exclaimed.

Yet this election left the most established democracy in the Middle East without a clear path to a new government. It produced an inconclusive result where neither opposing bloc will have a majority in parliament.
Some might say this was business as usual.
Israel has never had a one-party government. Its fragmented, proportional representation system is almost designed to govern by coalition.

Yet many commentators warned this election had revealed the fundamental and perhaps growing divisions that scar this nation. This was not a plebiscite in which an electorate united around a single cause.

How these vastly diverging views coalesce into some form of government is now the unenviable task facing Israel's body politic - the choices and compromises they may have to make could involve fundamental decisions about the country's future.

Would Netanyahu be ready to abandon his religious allies and form a coalition with right-wingers from the opposition bloc? Would they be ready to swallow their hostility towards the prime minister and sit in his government?

Is the opposition bloc ready to abandon much of its campaign promises and co-operate with Arab parties to force Netanyahu out of office? Are the Arab parties ready to risk joining a government that could fall within months?

Yair Golan, the left-wing Democrat leader, urged the opposition bloc to form a partnership with Arab parties. "We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said.
But are the people of Israel ready for such a reality?

Amit Segal, an Israeli commentator sympathetic towards Netanyahu, said the high turnout among Arab Israeli voters "reminded Jews on both sides that, after years of division, they may have to learn to sit together after all".

The risk is that this election, instead of putting Israel on a new path, has instead raised further doubts about what it is that unites its citizens. What are the common factors that bind this complex, varied collection of peoples into one polity?

Autocratic governments, which are growing in number, have long criticised democracies for producing weak and temporary governments, often fragile coalitions that struggle to hold together, let alone deliver what the people wanted.
Israel may now struggle for months to form a government. It might even fail and have to hold another election.
President Herzog acknowledged this risk head on as he prepared to open coalition negotiations: "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections."

For years, Israel has focused on defending itself against its external enemies. But must it also now be ready to defend itself from perils within, if the divisions writ large by this election become unmanageable?

In another speech, Churchill once said democracy was not just "insurance against dangers from abroad". It was also, he added, "insurance against dangers scarcely less grave and much more near and constant which threaten us here at home".
Can Israel's democracy live up to this challenge?

articles.title: Watch: King dances in the streets of the Bahamas capital
articles.summary: The monarch is in the Bahamas as part of a tour of the Caribbean during which he addressed the "great suffering of the past".

blocks.text: King Charles III danced in the street while taking part in a parade with officials in the Bahamas capital city of Nassau.
On Tuesday, the King gave a speech at an event celebrating local youth and acknowledged "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.
The nine-day tour will end in the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting, where the King says leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.

articles.title: US ambassador suggests Trump could blame Canada if midterms don’t go his way
articles.summary:
Pete Hoekstra, controversial US ambassador to Canada, has also accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections

The US ambassador Pete Hoekstra has suggested Canada could be blamed…

blocks.text: The US ambassador Pete Hoekstra has suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans perform poorly in next week’s midterm elections, the latest intervention from a controversial figure who has been accused of inflaming a bitter dispute that has angered and baffled residents of both countries.

On Wednesday, CTV news reported that Hoekstra told business leaders at a closed door meeting that if a number of swing races – including Maine and Michigan – go to the Democrats, it could make things harder for Canada because Donald Trump might try to blame the loss on it.
“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” the prime minister, Mark Carney, told reporters when asked about the allegations.
For months, Canada and the US have been locked in a bitter tariff war, with Ottawa retaliating against illegal US tariffs and targeting goods in states that rely heavily on trade with Canada.
Carney said that Canada “will pursue” such a deal if it presents itself, but that Ottawa’s trade negotiators are “not in that position right now”.

Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particular for his response to Trump’s rhetoric about making Canada the 51st US state. Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the threats as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”. He had previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election as “anti-American”.

This year a House of Commons petition signed by more than 225,000 Canadians called for his expulsion, suggesting his statements violated diplomatic protocols, including the prohibition on diplomats interfering in the internal affairs of a host country.

More recently, Hoekstra has accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections, pointing to Canadian politicians who have criticized the tariffs in US media, and the province of Ontario’s anti-tariff advertisement that ran on US television.

“We see all of that. We are monitoring it. We are evaluating it. And if some of it becomes election interference, America will respond to it,” Hoekstra, who comes from Michigan, recently told a Canadian podcast, adding that Canadians should “keep your nose out of American politics”.

Canada’s industry minister, Mélanie Joly, who was a target of Hoekstra’s comments, told reporters in Ottawa that her country “would never do that” and said Canada would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada”.
Carney, while in Turkey, told reporters there was “no merit” to the claims of interference and that he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.

Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, said the remarks were an “extraordinary thing” for a US ambassador to say about his host country and looked like an effort to “manufacture a pretext for the Trump administration’s own political difficulties”.
“The job of an ambassador is to represent the interests of his country, but it’s also to maintain channels of communication and build relationships and manage disagreements,” he said.

“His comments have repeatedly aggravated tensions instead of helping to manage them. I don’t think that he’s serving American interests very well. I’m not even sure that he’s serving the interests of his president.”

Paris points to polling in the US that shows voters have increasingly linked tariffs, the war and cost of living. There is also widespread confusion over why the White House has chosen to treat Canada as a trade adversary.

“It’s certainly not working in Canada. It’s on the contrary. It seems that every time Mr. Hoekstra opens his mouth, the Canadians are more determined than before to stand up to the bullying of the Trump administration,” he said. “That’s not serving American interests.”
The US embassy denied Hoekstra said Canada would face blame for a poor Republican showing, suggesting the remarks were “grossly taken out of context” from a broader discussion.

“The ambassador has consistently said that the Canadian media is attempting to overstate the relevance of Canadian issues in American elections. As we have previously stated, Americans will decide American elections based on issues that are important to them,” the embassy said in a statement.

At a Canadian American Business event last year, Hoekstra delivered what witnesses say was an expletive-laden tirade at Ontario’s trade representative after the province ran a series of anti-tariff ads in the US that featured Ronald Reagan. Ontario’s premier called the outburst “absolutely unacceptable” and “unbecoming of an ambassador”.

Last week, Barack Obama noted the unusual choice to attack a longtime ally while speaking at a Democratic campaign rally in Detroit, mocking Trump’s fixation on Canada and jokingly referring to his northern neighbor as a “well-known evil empire”.

“That historical adversary of ours: Canada,” the former US president said. “It’s your neighbor! It’s a few minutes drive over the bridge. These are the people who gave us Martin Short … and maple syrup. They are the nicest people. And somehow we’ve gotten them so mad.”

articles.title: Budget 2026: Healey hikes taxes on banks and landlords to fund £100 handouts to 20m households
articles.summary: Few surprises as chancellor uses low-key speech blaming ‘global economic storms’ for stoking energy prices and cost of living crisis
articles.byline: Heather StewartJessica Elgot and Richard Partington

blocks.text: John Healey raised taxes on banks and landlords to fund a £100 winter handout for 20 million families as official forecasts made clear there is no end in sight for the cost of living crisis.
In his first budget, the chancellor blamed “global economic storms” for the grim outlook, as the war in Iran drives up oil and gas prices.
But he also faced criticism for failing to squeeze more money from profitable banks, punishing savers and not giving enough help to the poorest.

In a low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, Healey was at pains to stress he was sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules, and there were few surprises in his hour-long address to MPs.

But with households facing soaring energy prices, and mortgage bills rising amid higher interest rates, Healey offered a £100 cost-of-living payout, which will be sent to all English households in council tax bands A-D.
