It formed the centrepiece of a cost of living package, which he said would “take the pressure off in the coldest months, and see people through to the spring”.
The £2.6bn cost of the £100 giveaway includes funding for the Scottish and Welsh governments, which Healey said he hoped they would use to implement a similar scheme.

“I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. I know that people look to government at times like this, not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space,” he said.

But the government’s independent forecaster warned households face a “grim picture” on living standards, as it slashed the outlook for the economy in 2027 and said there was “virtually no growth” in disposable income for households.

Healey also came under fire for an unexpected 2p increase in tax rates for income earned on property or savings. As well as hitting savers and landlords, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said it risks “leading to a steady rise in rents”, by deterring landlords from the market and cutting supply, as well as passing on costs to tenants.
Ruth Curtice, the chief executive of the Resolution Foundation thinktank, criticised the £100 handout, arguing it would have been better to give more generous support to the poorest consumers.
“The chancellor has missed the mark with badly targeted support that has left families facing a tough winter as energy bills rise,” she said.
As expected, the chancellor also cancelled fuel tax rises planned by Rachel Reeves, and extended the VAT cut on electricity prices previously announced to next summer.

Healey announced several measures intended to cut businesses’ costs – including raising the rates relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 for companies in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors. The change would be funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops, he said.
The cost of the household support measures will be met by a doubling of the additional levy banks pay on their profits, to 6%; as well as the higher taxes on income from property and savings.

The additional bank tax will only last for 15 months and marked a less significant rise than some in the industry had feared. Banks’ share prices were among the highest risers in the blue chip FTSE 100 index on Wednesday.
Laura Suter, director of personal finance at AJ Bell, said: “Savers will be hit with another hefty tax rise on their savings interest, adding to the squeeze on their savings over the past few years.”
She added that the higher tax on rental income “could be passed on to tenants, with rent hikes a potential lever for landlords to mitigate any increase in tax”.
“Equally, we could see yet more landlords selling up, in favour of investing their money in other assets that have lower taxes and less government tinkering,” she said.

The New Economics Foundation thinktank accused Healey of failing to be bold enough. Hannah Peaker, its deputy chief executive, said: “As households prepare to be hit by a wave of price rises this winter, the chancellor has shown the right instincts but not yet the right scale.
“The £100 support with energy bills will provide some welcome relief, but the chancellor could have been braver in the face of what we are up against.”
after newsletter promotion

Energy provider EdF predicts that the Ofgem price cap – which determines consumer bills – is set to go up by £466 in January. And despite Healey’s promise of a “breathing space,” in the teeth of the crisis, official forecasts published by the OBR alongside the budget pointed to a challenging winter.
Presenting the forecasts, the OBR’s David Miles highlighted a “pretty grim picture” for household finances, as inflation rises to almost 4%.

Even by 2030-31, it only expects real disposable household incomes – its favoured measure of living standards – to be 2% higher than before the Covid pandemic. It now expects anaemic economic growth of 1% next year, about half a percentage point lower than expected in March.

Healey said higher inflation and interest rates had hit the government’s finances too, ratcheting up the government’s interest bill by £14bn this year alone, but promised to stick to Labour’s fiscal rules.

The OBR said Healey would meet the most important rule – to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues – with a diminished headroom of £15bn by the target date of 2029-30, against the £24bn Rachel Reeves had built up in the spring.
Borrowing is scheduled to be higher than expected in the short term, but the chancellor promised to rebuild the buffer against the rules to £22bn by the end of the five-year forecast period.
“That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can,” he said. Bond markets appeared unruffled by the higher-than-expected borrowing.
The deferral of some important decisions to next year’s spending review prompted the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, to argue Burnham was keeping his options open on an early general election.

Burnham doubled down on his promise not to call one, however, telling reporters on Wednesday he could rule one out for at least 12 months. “I’m not thinking about my own party and its prospects. I am thinking about people, and I’m thinking about what I can do to help them.”

Badenoch said Britain had “overspent, overborrowed and overtaxed”, and criticised Healey for delayed decisions on defence spending and welfare cuts. Healey has said he will tackle welfare after reports from Alan Milburn on youth unemployment and Sir Stephen Timms on disability benefits, expected next month.

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned that by sticking to the tight spending plans bequeathed by Reeves, Healey could be storing up trouble for the crucial spending review due next year.

“History warns us to be sceptical of tight spending plans in later years of the forecast. Next year’s spending review will be a crunch point, and looks very tough for many departments, whose budgets will be squeezed by higher inflation forecasts,” she said.
“The plans for overall spending set out in the budget mean that spending choices at next year’s spending review will be much harder than those made so far this parliament.”

Buried in the budget was a hint at an easing of some migration restrictions, including some industries that will be allowed to lower the salary thresholds for visas to allow companies across the country to hire international talent.

Among the winners was London mayor Lord Sadiq Khan, who received new powers to extend the Bakerloo line in London and a pledge that cross-Channel trains will now also stop at Stratford International in east London. There was also cash to explore hosting the Olympics in “a northern city” – and former Greater Manchester mayor Burnham may have a candidate city in mind.

articles.title: Russell Brand tells trial it was wrong to use fame to ‘facilitate’ sex with women
articles.summary:
Former comedian, in court on rape and sexual assault charges, says he misused position but ‘consent is more important than sex itself’

Russell Brand has told a court that he was wrong to…

blocks.text: Russell Brand has told a court that he was wrong to have used his fame and success to “facilitate” sexual activity with women.
The 51-year-old comedian said he had “misused” his position “very selfishly” and dedicated his life to “reckless philandering and idiocy”.
But he insisted that “consent is more important than sex itself” and that the criminal case had been a “deeply traumatic episode” in his life.
Brand is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.
Wearing a dark suit, white shirt and tie, he appeared in the witness box for four hours on Wednesday as he gave evidence at Southwark crown court.
He said he had achieved “staggering fame” after marrying the US pop star Katy Perry in 2010 but that now nobody would “touch him with a bargepole”.

blocks.caption: Russell Brand denies all the charges. At the start of his evidence, he repeatedly said ‘no’ when the individual claims were put to him. Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA

blocks.text: He blamed his downfall on “devastating” 2023 media reports about his alleged sexual misconduct, which he said had led to him being barred from visiting his baby son when he was having open heart surgery at Great Ormond Street hospital.

He also said he had failed to persuade a single person with relevant information to give evidence on his behalf at his criminal trial. “Would they touch you with a bargepole?” his barrister, Ian Winter KC, asked. Brand replied: “No.”

The TV personality gave confident answers in a booming voice to Winter, issuing a series of terse “no” replies when asked if he had raped women in a hotel room, at his home and in a bar toilet, and sexually assaulted radio and TV workers.
He told the court he was “innocent” of all the charges and said: “Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself.”
He later added: “Consent is an ongoing process and at any point anybody can withdraw their consent.”
During the course of his evidence, Brand told the court he does not remember some of the incidents in the charges and remembers only consensual sexual encounters in others.
He admitted saving the telephone number of a woman who accuses him of anal rape in 2009 with the letter “T” next to her name, meaning “tart”.
The woman alleges Brand raped her at his north London townhouse, a few days after she had willingly engaged in a threesome with the star backstage at the Hammersmith Apollo venue in London.
When Winter asked what he meant by the word “tart”, he replied: “That was what I used to denote casual hook-ups.”
He also put two asterisks next to the woman’s name, which he told the jury meant: “Never, ever forget this individual, this is a memorable encounter.”

Brand used colourful language to describe some of his accusers. He described a woman who alleges he raped her at the Labour party conference in 1999 as “vivacious and loquacious” and an MTV worker who accuses him of oral rape in 2004 as having “prominent eyes”. “She was lithe, elfin, pixieish, energetic,” he said.

But there were tense moments during cross-examination in which Brand stared at the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, in silence for several seconds. Occasionally he could be seen moving his lips before speaking out loud.

The prosecutor probed him about alleged inconsistencies in his previous statements and what he has told the jury with regards to the woman who accused him of anal rape. Brand said: “Ms Karmy-Jones, I completely agree. Since these events occurred there’s been escalating recollection.
“It’s been a deeply traumatic episode of my life I’ve focused on at the expense of my marriage, my children and health. I ask your forgiveness, well, not your forgiveness.
“I recognise that this recollection includes small details that are inconsistent and I acknowledge that.”

And when asked if the young fan was “just another sexual conquest” in his attempt to sleep with 5,000 women, Brand told the court: “I really don’t know the number, but it’s difficult to dispute that’s how I conducted myself in the pursuit of willing sexual partners.”

As he came to the end of his cross-examination, Karmy-Jones challenged Brand on what he had done to upset the woman so much. “I think I was in a position of fame, a successful person who was admired and I misused that commodity very selfishly,” he said.

“You were in a position of power in respect of each of these women,” the prosecutor continued, to which Brand replied: “As I became more successful and famous I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong.”

Karmy-Jones also confronted him with extracts from his 2007 book, My Booky Wook, in which Brand said he “would never have relented until I received my birthright orgasm”. Responding to one of the passages, Brand said: “I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man.

“With women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I’ve been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering, and idiocy.”

The prosecutor said that Brand’s book included a picture of himself as a seven-year-old with the caption: “This is the exact moment when I decided to act gay to attract girls. It took 15 years to produce results.”
The first alleged rape victim has told the court she believed Brand was gay when they first met at a Labour party conference fringe event, which led to her agreeing for him to come to her hotel room.
The prosecutor asked Brand: “That’s something you would do, wasn’t it? That was something you would do to make girls trust you?”
“No,” Brand replied.

Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Mr Justice Bennathan told jurors they should find Brand not guilty of the indecent assault allegation after he concluded “there was insufficient evidence” to support the charge.
The trial continues.

articles.title: New Vera C. Rubin telescope spots possible new dwarf planet beyond Pluto
articles.summary: Scientists using a Chile-based telescope have identified an icy object orbiting beyond Pluto ‌that may join our solar system's small roster of dwarf planets.

image.caption: This image shows the orbital pathway of newly discovered dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 (ED138), as observed by NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. (NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA)

blocks.text: Science·New
Scientists using a Chile-based telescope have identified an icy object orbiting beyond Pluto ‌that may join our solar system's small roster of dwarf planets.
More observations are needed to confirm the discovery

Researchers said the candidate, named 2026 ED138, has a diameter estimated at between roughly 600 and 1,500 kilometres and is orbiting about 46 times farther from the sun than Earth. By way of comparison, ​Pluto orbits at an average of about 40 times farther from ​the sun than Earth.

The object was spotted using the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory, on the summit of the Cerro Pachón mountain in central Chile. The telescope is a joint ​initiative of the U.S. National Science Foundation and U.S. Department of Energy.
Further observations are ⁠needed to confirm that the ⁠object is a dwarf planet.

If confirmed, 2026 ED138 would ‌join five other dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union, the global authority on classifying celestial bodies. Those are Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake, all of which orbit beyond the outermost planet Neptune, and Ceres, located in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
Based on the current ⁠data, 2026 ED138 would be among the largest of the dwarf planets.

"For me, what this demonstrates is that many exciting discoveries remain to be made with the Rubin Observatory and other telescopes," said astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Center for ‌Astrophysics, Harvard & Smithsonian, who first spotted 2026 ED138.

items: NASA is launching the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Here are just a few of the wonders it will reveal
New giant telescope reveals its 1st images of our universe

blocks.text: Pluto long was considered the solar system's ninth and outermost planet, but was reclassified by the International Astronomical Union as a dwarf planet in 2006 because it did not meet the organization's formal definition of a planet. Pluto and the new dwarf planet candidate ​reside in a frigid region of the solar system populated by various icy bodies.
Questions remain

There are still questions about the size and composition of 2026 ED138. ⁠To be considered a dwarf planet, an object must possess sufficient mass for its own gravity to pull ⁠it into a round shape. 2026 ED138 appears to have sufficient mass for that, but more observations are ⁠needed.
"The ⁠main thing we need to do is ​to establish the physical size of 2026 ED138," Holman said.
See a swarm of new asteroids

"When we observe with Rubin, we are seeing the sun's ​light reflected from the object," Holman ⁠said. "A smaller, more reflective object would show the same amount of light as a larger, less reflective object. Fortunately, by looking at longer wavelengths, with an observatory like ALMA, we can detect the light emitted by the object itself," which is helpful in measuring an object's size.
ALMA, or the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, is a powerful telescope also based in Chile.
The ⁠discovery was announced at a ‌scientific meeting in Spokane, Wash.

articles.title: Politics live: Chalmers calls social media a ‘business model for hate’; half of young Australians say US a ‘threat’
articles.summary: • Get our breaking news email, free app or

blocks.text: Key events

items: 10m agoSocial media a ‘business model for hate’: Chalmers
10m agoWelcome

blocks.text: Australia’s immediate neighbours are trusted more than historic allies, according to a new survey AAP reports on, which shows the United States is increasingly considered a “threat”.

Only half of the Australians polled in a YouGov survey, commissioned by the Australia Institute, considered long-time ally the US a “friend”. Meanwhile 42% perceived America as a “threat” (defined as a nation viewed with caution or suspicion).

Two-thirds of One Nation voters perceive the US as a friend, with the Coalition close behind. Labor voters are largely split and only one-quarter of Greens voters view the global superpower positively.
Only 4% of young voters labelled the US a “close friend” while over half considered it a threat.

Only 21% of respondents had confidence in Donald Trump to “do the right thing” in world affairs, ahead of only Chinese president Xi Jinping, Russian president Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
Indonesia, a close geographic neighbour and emerging partner, has been rated a more trusted partner than the United States, leading by 14% in the friend category.
Social media a ‘business model for hate’: Chalmers

blocks.caption: Tom McIlroy

blocks.text: Tom McIlroy
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, says overheated discourse on social media is in large part responsible for the toxicity in politics, including the threats and abuse being sprayed at politicians.

Speaking at the Political Book of the Year awards in Canberra last night, Chalmers reflected on the alleged attack against Indi MP Helen Haines last week. He said hate had always been present in Australian society but it now has “a business model, a formula, an assembly line for mass-production.”
He described a new kind of digital misogyny that follows women in public life wherever they go, making the current climate harshest for women.

double quotation markThat climate is no accident. Hate is monetised and weaponised by algorithmic rage-bait. Extremism is incentivised; nuance is penalised. The most available public figures are the most vulnerable. So tonight is a little reminder of why reason and research matters, why nuance matters, what’s at risk and what’s at stake and why that matters too. Books inform our views without hardening them. Social media hardens our views without informing them.
Haines is recovering in hospital. Police have charged a 43-year-old man over the alleged attack outside her Wangaratta electorate office.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Kat Wong with the main action.

articles.title: Most cougar deaths in Alberta study were caused by people
articles.summary: A new study of cougar deaths in west-central Alberta found mortality risk was higher near residential areas and secondary roads and among cougars that frequently crossed human-made clearings. Of the…

image.caption: This image of a young cougar was captured by an Alberta Fish and Wildlife trail camera in the Hinton area. New research suggests roads, homes and other human-made corridors cutting through cougar habitats may affect not only where the animals go, but their chances of survival. (Alberta Fish and Wild

blocks.text: Science·New

A new study of cougar deaths in west-central Alberta found mortality risk was higher near residential areas and secondary roads and among cougars that frequently crossed human-made clearings. Of the 37 documented cougar deaths, 29 were caused by people.
Hunting was the leading cause of death among the cougars tracked
Patrick Cummins once had a cougar cross his backyard, climb onto his deck and walk across the roof of his home.
Cummins, who lives near Bergen, Alta., didn't see the cougar. He only saw its tracks in the snow.
In 51 years living on the property, Cummins has never seen a cougar there with his own eyes, though he has caught the elusive predators on trail cameras.
"We always knew there was cougars there," Cummins said. "I suppose we were sort of always looking over our shoulder a little bit, but they've never bothered anybody around here that I know of."
But tracks can make an otherwise invisible predator vulnerable.

A cougar crosses Patrick Cummins's property near Bergen, Alta., on Feb. 7. New research examines how the human footprint affects cougar survival in west-central Alberta. (Submitted by Patrick Cummins)
New research from west-central Alberta suggests roads, homes and other human-made corridors cutting through cougar habitat may affect not only where the animals go, but their chances of survival.

Researchers tracked 80 GPS-collared cougars over five years and found their mortality risk was higher when the animals were closer to homes and secondary roads and when they crossed human-made clearings more frequently.
Of 37 documented deaths, 29 were caused by people.
"I think that's just all about access for hunters, really," said Carter Littlefair, lead author of the study, published Wednesday in PLOS One.

Littlefair, who completed the research while a graduate student at the University of Alberta, said secondary roads can provide hunters with easier access to cougar habitat. Clearings can also reveal where the animals have travelled.
"If a cougar was to cross the road, it's going to leave tracks."
Cougars often avoid trails used by people, which is why the province hopes to reduce trail density in key wildlife areas. (Submitted Delaney Frame/Alberta Environment and Parks)
Human footprint linked to mortality risk
The study followed cougars between 2016 and 2021 across a landscape that included secondary roads and human-made clearings such as seismic lines, powerline corridors and railways.

Hunting was the largest single cause of death, accounting for 16 of the 37. Another eight cougars died after being caught in traps intended for other animals. Five others were killed in vehicle collisions or removals involving problem animals or by a landowner.
Researchers also found a large seasonal difference in survival. Estimated survival was 96 per cent from April through October, but 62 per cent from November through March.
2 cougar cubs found a home in Quebec. Now, they each need a name
Alberta's cougar hunting season during the study began Dec. 1 each year and ran through the end of February or until quotas were met.

The research found an association between cougar mortality risk and human-made features, but did not directly measure hunter activity. Littlefair said increased hunter access and the likelihood of detecting cougars could help explain the relationship.
CBC News requested comment from Alberta Forestry and Parks but did not receive a response by publication time.
What the findings mean for the population

Researchers estimated annual survival at about 60 per cent, which Littlefair said is similar to other hunted cougar populations. Hunting also accounted for a smaller share of mortality than in some other studies, he said.
The study did not estimate population size or reproduction, so researchers cannot say whether the population is growing, stable or declining.

items: Even low levels of backcountry recreation linked to fewer wolverines, study finds
Sask. survivor of crash with moose shares warning about road dangers from wildlife

blocks.text: Littlefair said the research provides insight into how cougars die, but cannot determine whether they are dying at an unsustainable rate.
For Cummins, the role people played in the deaths was unexpected.
"Yeah, that surprises me," he said.
"There's more people in the rural areas these days than there used to be," Cummins said. "So from that sense, maybe it's caused by more people being out in the bush."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Eric Michael Johnson is a senior writer and editor based in Vancouver. Before joining CBC, he was an award-winning science writer and editor. He holds a PhD in the history of science from the University of British Columbia. He can be reached at eric.johnson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski addresses jury at his fraud trial for first time, says he's innocent
articles.summary: Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski addressed the jury for the first time at his Toronto fraud trial, thanking them, in his brief closing statement Wednesday morning.

image.caption: Aiden Pleterski, seen heading into court earlier this month, addressed the jury for the first time at his Toronto fraud trial to make a brief closing statement on Wednesday. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski addressed the jury for the first time at his Toronto fraud trial, thanking them, in his brief closing statement Wednesday morning.
"I am the least qualified person here to give a closing statement," Pleterski said in Ontario Superior Court.
"However, that being said, I am innocent of these charges. That is why I pled not guilty. Had I not been forced to represent myself, that would have been proven. That's all I have to say."

Pleterski represented himself at his trial, where he only cross-examined the first of 14 witnesses the Crown called and decided not to call evidence in his defence or to testify himself. When asked by Justice Shaun Nakatsuru whether he had questions for several of the witnesses, he told the court he didn't know what to ask and, in one case, said that he needed a lawyer.

The 27-year-old is accused of fraud over $5,000. At the end of the Crown's case, they dropped a second charge of money laundering against Pleterski. He was charged after a lengthy police investigation in May 2024.

items: 'Crypto King' trial hears recording of Aiden Pleterski admitting $300M fund 'never existed'
'Crypto King' spent $16.3M of investor funds on cars, credit cards, jets, security, accountant testifies

blocks.text: Pleterski was no 'Crypto King': Crown
Before Pleterski addressed the court, Crown prosecutor Akshay Aurora gave his roughly 90-minute closing statement.

"Mr. Pleterski was no 'Crypto King.' Far from it. As it turns out he was no king at all. He was a thief. A thief who stole investor money and used it as he pleased. A thief who stole investor money using calculated lies," Aurora told the jury.
"As you've seen, he burned through that money … he lived his best life, all while his investors pleaded for updates on their money, only to be ignored."
Crown prosecutor Akshay Aurora, seen in this courtroom sketch, delivered a roughly 90-minute closing statement at Pleterski's fraud trial on Wednesday. (Pam Davies/CBC)

Aurora provided an overview of the Crown's evidence in his closing statement, emphasizing that none of the investors' funds went into the trading platform, FXChoice, on their investment contracts. Instead, the prosecutor said Pleterski used it to pay back other investors, buy cars, fly on private jets and rack up credit card bills.
"The truth, members of the jury, are in the numbers, and the numbers do not lie," Aurora said.
"The numbers tell us Mr. Pleterski used investor money as if it was his own to fund his lavish lifestyle."

Earlier in Pleterski's trial, a senior forensic accountant who reviewed his financial records testified that investors provided Pleterski with more than $36.3 million and none of those funds were ever sent to FXChoice.

Instead, Albert Ciorma from the Ontario Securities Commission said his forensic audit found Pleterski spent about $5.6 million on luxury vehicles, $4.9 million on credit card bills, $870,000 on travel and private jets and $598,000 on security.
'Crypto King' admits $300M account never existed in audio recording played at trial
Pleterski also gave nearly $3.7 million to his parents and took $609,000 in cash advances from a credit card, Ciorma said.
Altogether, those expenses total more than $16.3 million. Pleterski also paid out another $16.1 million to investors from the funds he received, according to Ciorma.
Investor paid back own money
In his closing, Aurora walked jurors through some of the financial summaries Ciorma created of Pleterski's accounts as they related to about half of the dozen investors who testified at trial.

items: 'Crypto King' tells court he fears he might soon end up in jail cell with his kidnappers
Real estate developer testifies he gave 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski $4.5M to invest

blocks.text: In one case, the Crown showed how investor and witness Sacha Singh provided Pleterski with $1.3 million to invest, how that money made up almost all the funds in the account and that Singh was later paid back $700,000 of his own money from the same account.
Sacha Singh testified remotely by Zoom at Pleterski fraud trial on Oct. 14. (Pam Davies/CBC)

The prosecutor's examples also showed hundreds of thousands of dollars of investor funds being deposited in Pleterski's various accounts, only to be quickly withdrawn to pay other investors, credit card bills and go toward cars and a luxury home.
"None of the money went to MyFXChoice. You've seen it. Each time, Mr. Pleterski just uses the money as if it was his own," said Aurora in reference to these accounts.
Pleterski's investments were all failures
The Crown's closing also highlighted details on Pleterski's limited trading in cryptocurrency and foreign exchange over the course of the alleged fraud between July 2020 and July 2022.

"Every single investment account of Mr. Pleterski's is a failure and only generates losses," said Aurora. "$4,000 is all that comes into his account from any form of cryptocurrency or foreign exchange source."

items: 'Crypto King' investor recounts the moment he learned $311M investment fund didn't exist
'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski spent investors' money on exotic cars, private jet flights: Crown

blocks.text: Over the course of the trial, the jury heard about a purported $311 million fund in a FXChoice account — and how Pleterski provided screenshots and a video of it to concerned investors worried about their money in the spring of 2022.

Earlier this month, the jury in Pleterski's trial was shown this photo of Mitchell Learning holding his own phone with a screenshot the investor testified Pleterski sent him of Pleterski's trading account with a balance of more than $311 million. (Ontario Superior Court of Justice)

It came up in the testimony of several witnesses, alongside the screenshots and videos. Including one of Pleterski's email account, showing the FXChoice account where the money was supposed to be, had been deleted. The jury also heard an audio recording of a meeting with investors where Pleterski admitted the $311 million fund never existed.
'Every dollar was a decision he made'

"Who would delete a $300 million account? You wouldn't even delete a $300 account. It's clear that Mr. Pleterski was deleting that account because his 'investment scheme' was going to be unravelled … that it was going to be exposed," said Aurora in his closing statement.
"At no point, no point in the history of this account, was there $300 million, not even close. The highest this account was at was at $12,000."
The Crown also emphasized Pleterski knew he was deceiving investors from the beginning.
Ontario Superior Court Justice Shaun Nakatsuru is presiding over Pleterski's trial. (Pam Davies/CBC)
"Mr. Pleterski was the architect of this scheme. He controlled everything," Aurora told the jury.
"Every dollar spent was a decision he made. He was the architect. It would be impossible to say he did not know what he was doing."
As a result, the prosecutor told the jury Pleterski is guilty of fraud over $5,000.
Nakatsuru began giving his instructions to the jury late Wednesday morning and is expected to continue into the afternoon.
The judge told the jury they wouldn't start their deliberations until Thursday.

articles.title: How do the US midterms work, and why are they so important for Trump's presidency?
articles.summary: US voters are electing a new Congress. The results will be decisive for the future of the United States, and a judgment on Donald Trump's second term as president.

image.caption: Can the Republicans hang on to their majority in Congress?Image: Blake Fagan/AFP

blocks.text: On November 3, United States citizens will vote in the midterm elections. These won't decide who gets to sit in the White House; instead, Americans will be voting on who they want to see in the Capitol.

Midterm elections are held every four years, at the exact halfway point between presidential elections. The people of the United States decide who will represent them in the two chambers of the US Congress, the House of Representatives and the Senate. Some states are also voting for their governor. These are the decisions on the ballot paper — but they are not the only thing voters will be taking into account.

J. Miles Coleman, an election analyst at the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, explained before the last midterms that they were "often a referendum on the president and party currently in power." If the people are content, the party of the leader in the White House does better than if the people are predominantly dissatisfied. President Donald Trump's approval ratings are currently at a record low.

blocks.caption: President Donald Trump's approval ratings have sunk to an all-time low: More than 60% of Americans view him negativelyImage: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Who are Americans electing in the midterms?

All the seats in the US House of Representatives are up for election. Its 435 members are elected by eligible voters across the country. Each member represents one electoral district. These are allocated based on population size. As a result, relatively large US states where few people live, such as Wyoming, have only one seat in the House of Representatives. New Jersey, a much smaller state by surface area but with a larger population, has 12. Representatives are elected for a two-year term of office.

US senators, on the other hand, are elected for a six-year term. The Senate, the other chamber of the US Congress, has 100 seats: two for each of the 50 US states, regardless of size. Around one third of these senatorial seats come up for election every two years. This year there are 35, meaning that not every state will be electing a senator in these midterms.

Separately, voters in 36 states will elect their governor, whose term of office is four years in most states. Many decisions in the US are taken at state level, on everything from abortion law to education and electoral procedure. It can therefore make a considerable difference to people's lives whether Democrats or Republicans are the ones making these decisions in their state.
Who currently has a majority in the US Congress?
At present, the Republicans, the party of President Trump, have a majority in both houses of Congress — but its margin is slim.

The House of Representatives currently has 218 Republican deputies, 214 Democrats, and one independent, who usually votes with the Republicans. Two seats are vacant. Observers think it likely that the Democrats will seize the majority in this chamber in the upcoming elections. "It would be a surprise if the Democrats don't at least take the House [of Representatives]," Coleman told the American broadcaster CBS at the end of October.

In the Senate there are currently 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats, and two independent senators who usually vote with the Democrats. When a vote in the Senate is deadlocked 50:50, the US vice president has the deciding vote. This means that currently, Trump's Vice President JD Vance would tip the scales if there were a tie in a Senate vote.

blocks.caption: Republicans and Democrats are vying for seats in the two chambers of the US CongressImage: Graeme Sloan/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why are the midterms so important?

Voter turnout is typically lower for midterms than for presidential elections, but the results will decisively influence US politics for the next few years. Despite the significant executive power delegated to the presidency, the majority of federal political decisions have to be approved by Congress before they can be implemented.

It is therefore considerably easier for Trump to govern the country as he chooses if the Republicans have a majority in both chambers of Congress. If the Democrats win a majority in one or both chambers, it will be more difficult for him to make changes to either domestic or foreign policy.
Which races are crucial?

The Democrats only need to win four more seats in the House of Representatives to gain a majority. They would then have 218 representatives. Out of the 435 races, only a few are still considered toss-ups. These include districts in Iowa, Virginia and Montana.

One senatorial race to watch is the one in Texas. Current polls put Democrat James Talarico level with his Republican rival, Ken Paxton. The Democrats need four more seats in the Senate to win a majority. The possibility that Texas could be one of them is already a sensation. No Democrat has won here at state level since 1994. Talarico now even has the support of some members of the Bush family, the Texas Republican dynasty of former presidents George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush, his son.
Many US voters are undecided, disillusioned or disengaged

In the gubernatorial elections it is possible that, for the first time in US history, a Black woman could become state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the Black Republican Lisa DeMuth are vying for the position, while in Georgia the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is up against the Republican Rick Jackson.

DeMuth is unlikely to win in Minnesota: The state generally votes Democrat, and Klobuchar, who has been state senator there for almost two decades, is much better known than her rival. In Georgia, however, the latest polls suggest it's neck-and-neck. Bottoms has a realistic chance of winning.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Israel’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalition
articles.summary:
Incumbent could turn defeat into another term in office as rival parties erect confected barrier to unseating him

Hours before the final results from

blocks.text: Hours before the final results from Israel’s elections were in, several things were clear. Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition had lost its mandate, and the opposition had a firm majority.

But most of Israel’s Jewish opposition ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties, in the course of a racist election campaign in which Netanyahu painted Palestinian citizens as an enemy inside the state.

The self-imposed ban on a broader opposition alliance, if it holds, offers Netanyahu the prospect of turning his defeat into another term in office – or at least a prolonged mandate as caretaker prime minister and perhaps another round of elections.

This confected barrier to unseating Netanyahu became the focus of Israeli media and analysts. “No Clear Government” announced the newspaper Israel Hayom. “Road to Unity Government Has Been Paved”, read an article on Channel 12.

Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, attacked that framing. “Netanyahu lost. I know how to count,” he said in a statement calling for a government with Palestinians, who make up about 20% of Israel’s population.

“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said. “We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Arab citizens of Israel.”

blocks.caption: Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra’am party, holds his daughter as he casts his vote in Maghar, Israel. Photograph: Rami Shlush/Reuters

blocks.text: Other Israelis were even more direct. “If you stop being racist two amazing things will happen to you,” musician Yali Sobol wrote in a Facebook post. “First, you will stop being racist. Second, you will discover you have won.”
While Palestinian-led parties do not describe themselves as Zionist, neither do some of the ultra-Orthodox groups who are a key part of Netanyahu’s current coalition.

A survey taken as polls closed on election day showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with the Palestinian-led Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu, political psychology researcher Eran Halperin said.
But opposition leaders were silent on Wednesday, as they apparently tried to balance their desire to unseat Netanyahu with promises against working with Palestinians.

Former general Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the biggest opposition party, has not directly ruled out governing with Palestinians but laid out conditions that made it politically impossible for them to join a coalition.

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot waves to supporters at an election night rally. Photograph: Noam Galai/Getty Images

blocks.text: Palestinians have been clearer about their priorities. “We are ready and prepared to pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government,” Yousef Jabareen, leader of the larger Joint List, said on Wednesday. “The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership.”
The Islamist Ra’am party put a Jewish former police chief in second position on their slate, in a signal of their commitment to working with Jewish Israelis.

A precedent from three decades ago, when Yitzhak Rabin relied on Palestinian support for a minority government as he sought a negotiated end to the Israel-Palestine conflict, gets little mention in contemporary Israeli political debate.
Netanyahu put racism at the heart of his campaign, in a strategy critics said was designed both to bolster voter support and complicate post-election coalition negotiations for the opposition.
A slogan featured on many of his election posters, “The right or Palestine”, framed 20% of the population as an enemy within Israel’s borders.

On election night he shrugged off the loss of about 10 seats from the 64 seat-coalition he assembled in 2022 – a severe rebuke from voters by most counts – to claim that his vision for Israel had been vindicated in the poll.

The Knesset overall has shifted further right, as have young Israelis, and after the results came in, he issued an open invitation to put their opposition to Palestinian parties ahead of their opposition to him.
“The rightwing bloc has a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public,” he said. “We must form a strong national-right government”.

Many in Israel described this election as existential, as they struggled to halt the erosion of democracy inside Israel’s pre-1967 borders, and secure a State Commission of Inquiry into the 7 October attacks.

For Palestinian citizens facing surging crime, discrimination and home demolitions inside Israel and watching family and friends endure ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank and a war of annihilation in Gaza, that was viscerally true, and they came out in record numbers.

Israel describes itself as a Jewish and democratic state. If the representatives of Palestinians are now effectively excluded from government because of their race, Netanyahu will have turned that promise into more of a choice – between a Jewish future or a democratic one.

articles.title: How did Flávio Bolsonaro end up in Miami?
articles.summary: BBC Verify has pieced together defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro's journey through Brazil, Argentina and Ecuador to reach Miami.

blocks.text: Brazil's defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro has landed in the US after ongoing uncertainty about his whereabouts.
The US state department told the BBC on Tuesday it will issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family.
BBC Verify has pieced together his journey through Brazil, Argentina and Ecuador to reach Miami.
Produced by Jenna Abaakouk. Graphics by Sally Nicholls.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after defeat in Brazil's presidential election
articles.summary: His arrival in the US ends speculation about his whereabouts after he failed to comply with an order to surrender his passports.
articles.byline: Vanessa Buschschlüter, Ione Wells, Max Matza

blocks.text: Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro has flown to Miami after losing the country's presidential election on Sunday.
His arrival in Florida ends days of confusion over his whereabouts, after he was reported to have travelled to Argentina, and then prematurely reported to have already entered the US on Tuesday.

The US has said it would grant visas to Bolsonaro and his family, who travelled with him. Brazil cancelled his passport, after he failed to surrender it to authorities, due to an ongoing criminal investigation. He has denied any wrongdoing.
Newly reelected President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has criticised the departure, saying "those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear".

Speculation about Bolsonaro's whereabouts was first triggered by a report on an Argentine news site, which claimed that he had crossed the land border between Brazil and Argentina and then boarded a private plane en route to the US.

Brazilian police took the rumours seriously. Early on Tuesday, they checked border crossings but found no evidence that Bolsonaro had left the country, and Argentine officials said they had no reports of him crossing.
For a little while, it seemed like Bolsonaro may just be keeping an uncharacteristically low profile after being unexpectedly beaten by his left-wing rival in the presidential run-off vote on Sunday.
When he failed to surrender his passports in time to meet a 24-hour deadline, Brazilian authorities cancelled the documents and ordered police to make checks at border posts.
With Bolsonaro's lawyers saying they did not know where he was, speculation quickly grew again that he might have left the country.
Flávio Bolsonaro is not the first member of his family to travel to the United States.
His father, Jair Bolsonaro, also left Brazil for Florida in December 2022 before his successor, President Lula, was inaugurated.

Jair was still in the US when his supporters stormed Brazil's government buildings and Supreme Court on 8 January. He later used his absence as part of his defence in his coup trial, which led to a conviction and 27-year sentence.

Eduardo Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has been living in Texas after taking leave from Brazil's Congress. While in the US, he lobbied officials there in an attempt to influence the coup trial of his father, which led to the US imposing punitive tariffs on Brazil and sanctions on key officials.
Eduardo was convicted in absentia over this by Brazil's highest court earlier this year.
It is not yet clear what Flávio Bolsonaro's ultimate destination will be, nor how long he plans to stay in the US.
He is the subject of two investigations currently pending before Brazil's Supreme Federal Court.
One is regarding possible irregularities in the transfer of nearly $70m (£53m) from private bank Banco Master to the film Dark Horse – a biopic about his father.
The second investigation relates to alleged money laundering, both of which Bolsonaro denies.
He is set to lose his parliamentary immunity on 31 January, when his eight-year Senate term ends.

articles.title: Vladimir Putin hails Elon Musk’s ‘genius’ amid plans for Russian Starlink
articles.summary:
Russia plans to build own version of US billionaire’s satellite communications to help attack Ukraine

Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s genius and said he was in touch with Starlink’s…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor

blocks.text: Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s genius and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine.

The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk’s SpaceX with Russia’s gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation.

“Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Russian leader said, according to the Tass news agency. “How many of these [satellites] does he have in orbit? More than 5,000, and we’re only taking the first steps.”

The true number of active SpaceX satellites is estimated at about 10,000, which provide the high-speed internet service that has been the subject of a diplomatic row between Musk, the US and Ukraine earlier this month.

A military version of Starlink, called Starshield, was suddenly restricted one night in the middle of October, preventing Ukraine from conducting medium drone attacks and hampering some of its anti-drone air defences.

Initially, Musk, an ally of the US president, Donald Trump, denied that he had ordered a throttling of the internet connection, before saying at the end of last week that he had closed a loophole in which the civilian Starlink had been used by the military.

Putin appeared to be trying to flatter Musk, whose control of the communications technology has raised questions about the US billionaire’s leverage over the White House and the impact he is able to have on Ukraine’s war effort.

blocks.caption: Elon Musk is a controlling shareholder in Starlink and an ally of Donald Trump. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters

blocks.text: “We are in close contact with our American partners – including Mr Musk – because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and ​to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin said.

Starlink does not work in Russia and its use by Russia inside Ukraine was restricted earlier this year. Meanwhile, Moscow has begun to develop an alternative system, though, with an estimated 26 working satellites, its capacity is limited.

Last week, after about 10 days of restriction, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, announced that “Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored” and that the speeds were “now where they need to be”.

Few believe the issue is permanently settled, with relations between Zelenskyy and Trump fraught in the run-up to the US midterm elections next Tuesday. Trump has also reached out to Putin, agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow early in October in an effort to reduce the oil price before Americans go to the polls.

Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he hoped proposed trilateral peace talks, involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, would take place between 6 and 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE, shortly after the midterms.

“We are waiting for the American side. I think that they’ll be ready with all the answers after the elections,” the Ukrainian leader said at a press conference in The Hague with the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten.
after newsletter promotion

Earlier, Zelenskyy said he had spoken to Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, as it emerged that Britain would provide £10bn in extra financing for Ukraine over the next three years – and an immediate £500m for air defence systems.

The additional aid was, Zelenskyy said, “a truly strong and very timely step” that came “as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone” as the war heads towards what is expected to be its most difficult winter yet.

John Healey, the UK chancellor, announced the extra funding as part of the government’s annual budget. “The prime minister and I called President Zelenskyy to tell him about our commitments in the budget today. He told us: ‘You’ve made my day’.”

The Dutch government also said it would provide €500m in military support for the winter, and a further €1.2bn in non-military aid, partly to help fund urgent repairs to Ukraine’s utilities and manufacturing.
Kyiv has been relentlessly attacked by Moscow this autumn as Russian forces fail to make progress on the frontlines in the east of Ukraine.

Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since the middle of October, Zelenskyy said overnight, hitting power plants and other key targets in an effort to cause a humanitarian crisis in the capital.

articles.title: ‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of Spain’s second deadly train crash in 10 months
articles.summary:
Passengers describe carriages full of seriously injured people after crash that has claimed at least 68 lives

Josimar Medina woke a little before 9am on Wednesday to find himself airborne…

blocks.text: Josimar Medina woke a little before 9am on Wednesday to find himself airborne and hurtling through his carriage on the fast train from Madrid to Seville.
“I remember flying through the air and looking for my girlfriend, who was also shooting through the air,” said Medina, a 37-year-old tourist from the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo.
Once he landed, he looked around and realised just how lucky he and his girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, had been.

“I saw people with cuts, people covered in blood, people missing limbs, and I saw one person who had nothing left below the chest,” said Medina. “I saw people with their heads crushed and people with mutilated arms.”

blocks.caption: Josimar Medina and his girlfriend Vitoria Maia, from Peru and Brazil respectively, were thrown across their carriage of the fast train from Madrid to Seville after it collided with another train on the track. Photograph: Sam Jones/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Peruvian stood recounting the details of Wednesday’s deadly rail crash, in which at least 68 people were killed and dozens more were injured, wearing a light brown T-shirt stained with the blood of a young American man he had helped move to safety.

Medina and Maia had been in the seventh carriage of the state-operated Renfe train that smashed into the back of a train run by the private Iryo company on the same line from the capital to the south of Spain. Had they been any further forward, they could well have been among the accident’s fatalities.

As it was, the couple climbed out of the train and helped the injured while they waited for medics and Guardia Civil officers to arrive at the scene of the crash, which took place amid vineyards and olive groves near the small town of Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, near the city of Toledo.

Within hours of the crash, Urda had been transformed into a frantic emergency response centre, with a local sports centre pressed into service as a triage post for the walking wounded. Cars, vans and trucks from the emergency services in Castilla-La Mancha and neighbouring Madrid crowded the streets.

blocks.caption: A member of the Spanish Red Cross embraces a woman as they wait for news of passengers on the two high-speed trains that collided near Urda. Photograph: Susana Vera/Reuters

blocks.text: Fredrich and Arabella Barilea, a couple from the Philippines who now live in Dubai, were on the Iryo train, and Fredrich was sent flying by the impact.

“One guy was shouting, ‘Get out! Get out! Another train could hit!” said Fredrich. “We saw all the people were also getting off. Many of them had head injuries and were covered in blood. We just got as far away from the train as we could.”
Eventually, buses arrived to ferry the lightly injured survivors to Urda – although the Barileas said they were too shocked and confused to know where exactly they had been brought.

“It all happened in a split second,” said Arabella. “The table we were sitting at just disappeared in the crash. I feel like we’re on our second life. You never know what could happen. We’re very grateful.”

blocks.caption: Frederich and Arabella Barilea, originally from the Philippines but currently living in Dubai, were passengers on the Iryo train that the fast train from Madrid hit from behind.  Photograph: Sam Jones

blocks.text: Around the couple, people queued patiently on the street as they waited to board coaches. Wearing torn and bloodstained clothes and, in some cases, bandages on their heads, they stared, mute and uncomprehending. Spain may have been in mourning, as the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said during his visit to Urda, but many of those fortunate enough to survive Spain’s second fatal rail crash in less than a year were still too deep in shock to begin grieving.

Ata Yelkaya, a young tourist from Turkey, usually takes the bus when he travels around Spain. On Wednesday, however, he had decided to try the Iryo. Sleepy and assuming his train had come to a halt at a station, he had switched off his tablet and pulled up his hood in preparation for a nap. At 8.53am, he felt what he would later learn was the impact of the Renfe train smashing into the carriages behind him.

“I woke up with a bump and hit my head on the seat in front of me,” he said, “I looked across at an elderly couple near me and saw that the woman had a cut in her eyebrow. That’s when I knew something serious had happened.”

blocks.caption: A passenger rescued from one of the trains involved in the collision in Urda. Photograph: Andrea Comas/AP

blocks.text: When he looked out of the window, he saw the carriages behind his – carriage No 5 – had come off the track and that many people had been killed or injured.

“Everyone was in shock but I tried to help other people get off the train,” he said. “I’m from Turkey and I lived through the 2023 earthquake there, so I stayed calm and tried to think about what to do and how to get out. It was only when I got out and saw some of the dead people that it hit me. I think everyone was in shock; too shocked even to panic or to scream.”

Wednesday’s disaster stirs memories of the Adamuz rail crash in January, in which 46 people died. Once again, a small town has found itself at the centre of a national disaster and, once again, local people have rallied to help, bringing food and water to a hall that had been set up as a centre for those searching for their relatives.

blocks.caption: Medical staff converted a nearby sports centres into a temporary medical facility. Photograph: Andrea Comas/AP

blocks.text: But, as also happened at Adamuz, the solidarity and kindness on display is likely to turn to anger over the coming hours as people seek answers as to how one of Europe’s most modern and extensive high-speed rail networks could experience two deadly accidents that have between them claimed at least 114 lives in the space of just 10 months. With a snap general election just a month away, many voters could use their votes to register their fury over another rail disaster. The “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash – as Spain’s transport minister has called them – will need to be explained as swiftly thoroughly as possible.

For all the rush to action and unity on display, there was also a sickening sense of deja vu. One woman from Urda, who had spent the morning driving people to town from the crash site, had few words to describe what she had seen and heard.
“Mejor no verlo,” she said – “it’s better not to see something like this”. Again.

articles.title: SWS: Sara Duterte's defense gets higher net satisfaction than prosecution
articles.summary: Thirty-five percent of adult Filipinos are dissatisfied, while 30 percent are satisfied "that the prosecution of the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte is being done in a just…

blocks.text: Thirty-five percent of adult Filipinos are dissatisfied, while 30 percent are satisfied "that the prosecution of the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte is being done in a just manner," according to a Social Weather Stations (SWS) survey released on Wednesday.
Twelve percent were very satisfied, and 18% were somewhat satisfied. Another 21% were somewhat dissatisfied, and 14% were very dissatisfied. The remaining 36% were undecided.

The September 21 to 27 survey, fielded before the House prosecution dropped three of the four articles of impeachment, yielded a net satisfaction rating of -5 for the prosecution, based on the difference between the percentage of satisfied and dissatisfied respondents.
Meanwhile, 47% of respondents were satisfied with the fairness of Duterte's defense by her lawyers, while 24% were dissatisfied, resulting in a net satisfaction rating of +23.
Background

The Third Quarter 2026 Social Weather Survey was conducted using face-to-face interviews of 1,500 adults nationwide: 600 in Balance Luzon (or Luzon outside Metro Manila) and 300 each in Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao. The sampling error margins are ±3% for national percentages, ±4% for Balance Luzon, and ±6% each for Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao.
The survey was non-commissioned.

On October 13, 2026, the Senate impeachment court granted the prosecution’s motion to drop Articles I, III, and IV, leaving only Article II, on unexplained wealth. The defense is scheduled to begin presenting its evidence when the trial resumes on November 9, 2026.
Estrada, Corona trials
According to SWS, net satisfaction with the prosecution is lower than in the trials of then President Joseph Estrada and Supreme Court Chief Justice Renato Corona.
During the Estrada impeachment trial, net satisfaction with the prosecution was +19 (41% satisfied, 22% dissatisfied) in December 2000 and +21 (42% satisfied, 21% dissatisfied) in January 2001.
During the impeachment trial of then-Chief Justice Renato Corona, it was +39 (54% satisfied, 15% dissatisfied) in March 2012.
Except during the Corona trial, net satisfaction was always lower with the prosecution than with the defense, SWS said.
Four accusations
"Asked about the four accusations against Vice President Duterte, more said they do not believe than believe each one, with net belief scores ranging from -9 to -21," SWS reported.
On the misuse of P612.5 million in confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education, 29% believed it and 38% did not, for a net belief score of -9.
On unexplained wealth that was not fully declared in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), 25% believed it and 38% did not, for a net belief score of -12.
On the bribery of Department of Education officials in connection with procurement irregularities, 27% believed it and 39% did not, for a net belief score of -12.

On the threat to have President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez assassinated, 23% believed it and 44% did not, for a net belief score of -21.
Around 26% to 30% were undecided on each accusation, while 7% had not heard or read about it, SWS said.
Face the trial
Meanwhile, 78% say it is important for the Vice President to testify personally.

Asked how important it is that Vice President Duterte testifies personally to be able to answer and explain all allegations against her, 78% said it is important: 59% definitely important and 19% somewhat important.
Only 15% said it is not important: 7% somewhat not important and 8% definitely not important. The remaining 8% did not know enough to give an opinion.

SWS said this was similar to the 78% in December 2000 and 79% in January 2001 who said it was important that then-President Estrada testify personally, and to the 73% in March 2012 and 81% in May 2012 who said the same of then-Chief Justice Corona [Chart 8].
"The earlier surveys used a two-point scale (important, not important), so the comparison is only indicative," SWS said. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Montreal grandparent scammer who fled to Central America pleads guilty in U.S. court
articles.summary: Jimmy Ylimaki, a Montreal man accused of defrauding American seniors as part of an elaborate grandparent scam network, has pleaded guilty in a U.S. court.

image.caption: Jimmy Ylimaki, seen here in a photo that appears in a court file in connection with a grandparent scam investigation, has pleaded guilty to participating in a grandparent scam conspiracy. (Matthew Lapierre/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal
Jimmy Ylimaki, a Montreal man accused of defrauding American seniors as part of an elaborate grandparent scam network, has pleaded guilty in a U.S. court.
Jimmy Ylimaki scammed American seniors as part of an elaborate network
Ylimaki, who was apprehended in Nicaragua earlier this year after spending a year as a fugitive, initially pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to commit fraud.
He changed his plea at a hearing on Oct. 19. He will be sentenced in January and faces up to 20 years in prison.
There are currently 31 other defendants accused alongside Ylimaki. They are being charged in the U.S., but remain in Canada, contesting extradition.

Prosecutors allege that scheme netted tens of millions of dollars. The alleged leader of the scam, Gareth West, appeared to run a real estate investment business, buying and selling property across Ontario and Quebec — while also posing as an influencer and amateur bodybuilder.
Meanwhile, co-conspirators, including Ylimaki, allegedly placed calls to elderly victims at call centres run by West, located around the Montreal area.
On the run in Central America

Ylimaki was caught “red-handed” in one of several raids police conducted against alleged call centres in the Montreal area in June 2024, according to U.S. assistant district attorney Nathanael Burris.
He was placing calls to U.S. seniors in the moments before police arrived. They found him hiding in a downstairs shower, at a building owned by West.
Shortly after the raid, which didn’t immediately lead to charges, Ylimaki left for Costa Rica.

items: Montreal grandparent scammer spent victims' money on cocaine, cars and parties: court documents

blocks.text: Then, in March 2025, police arrested two dozen people in the Montreal area and charged them with fraud-related offences, but West and Ylimaki evaded arrest.
Months later, West was arrested at an Airbnb in Saint-Colomban, Que., in July 2025.
Ylimaki was the only member of the alleged group of scammers who was still at large.
If you know anyone involved in this case, please contact Matthew Lapierre at matthew.lapierre@cbc.ca.
In the summer of 2025, a source with knowledge of Ylimaki's movements told CBC he was living in a coastal city in Costa Rica.
U.S. authorities were also tracking him.

In a motion for detention, filed in March 2026, Burris says Ylimaki — fearing he would be arrested and brought to the U.S. — began researching extradition proceedings involving Costa Rica and learned that the country collaborated with the U.S. on extradition matters. But neighbouring Nicaragua had historically refused U.S. extradition requests.
Tracking a Montrealer with alleged ties to a grandparent scam on the run in Central America
So, he crossed the border, according to Burris's filing.
It did not protect him. In March 2026, U.S. authorities said they had “apprehended” him in Nicaragua and “removed” him to the U.S. The details of that operation remain murky.
Ylimaki was a 'closer'
U.S. prosecutors have said Ylimaki participated in the scam as a “closer” — someone who posed as an attorney representing victims’ family members.
He convinced victims that they needed to provide a large sum of cash, thousands or tens of thousands of dollars, to bail their family member out of jail.
In his role, over just a 67-week period within the alleged three-year conspiracy, Ylimaki was paid more than $367,000 US.

“Moreover, members of the conspiracy in which Jimmy participated frequently transacted in cryptocurrency, making it difficult to ascertain the true extent of Jimmy’s resources,” Burris wrote in his March 2026 filing.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Matthew Lapierre is a journalist at CBC Montreal. He previously worked for the Montreal Gazette and the Globe and Mail. He can be reached at matthew.lapierre@cbc.ca and at mlapierre.07 on Signal.
